studies.location: Charité - Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Institute for Medical Immunology, Berlin

papers.title: Muscle symptoms and a latent physiological symptom-dysregulation factor in ME/CFS: exploratory analyses by sex and age-defined menopausal-status proxy group
papers.authors: Habermann-Horstmeier L, Horstmeier LM
papers.summary: Using the same large German survey as their earlier papers (745 people with ME/CFS), the authors found that muscle problems such as weakness and pain occur together with breathing problems, heart and blood-pressure symptoms, problems with temperature control, vision and digestion. This package looked the same regardless of how long someone had been ill. It differed somewhat between women and men and before and after menopause.
papers.why: ME/CFS symptoms form a recognisable whole-body pattern. Sex and menopause status should be considered when grouping patients for drug trials.

papers.title: DNA methylation: unifying framework for complex chronic conditions
papers.authors: Sharma, Rodger, Chatterjee, Tate et al.
papers.summary: This review looks at DNA methylation, chemical tags that switch genes on or off, in ME/CFS, long COVID, fibromyalgia and hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. These conditions share many symptoms, and the authors think they may share a biological root.
papers.why: The authors argue for studying these conditions together, which could lead to shared biomarkers and treatment targets.

papers.title: Can Depression Polygenic Risk Score Predict Postinfective Fatigue Syndrome (PIFS) in the Dubbo Infection Outcomes Study (DIOS)?
papers.authors: Ruseva AG, Valencia BM, Gordon SD, Lloyd A, Hickie IB, Martin N
papers.summary: Researchers followed 464 people after a confirmed infection such as glandular fever to see who developed postinfective fatigue syndrome, a CFS-like illness, six months later. They tested whether inherited genetic risk for depression or for chronic fatigue syndrome predicted who became ill.
papers.why: Neither genetic risk score predicted the illness. That argues against the idea that post-infective ME/CFS-like illness is hidden depression. A weak hint that depression risk genes raise the odds in women and lower them in men needs a larger study.

papers.title: Shared Clinical and Immunological Features of Post-Acute COVID-19 and Post-Acute COVID-19 Vaccination Syndromes
papers.authors: Dinser J, Anft M, Wiemers L, Skrzypczyk S, Kohut E, Kurek J, Stervbo U, Seibert FS, Westhoff TH, Rosiewicz K, Babel N
papers.summary: A German team compared people with lasting fatigue and other symptoms after a COVID-19 infection with people whose similar symptoms began after a COVID-19 vaccination. Both groups had similar autoantibodies against stress-hormone and nerve receptors. Many still had spike protein, a piece of the virus or vaccine, in their blood, especially those whose symptoms began after vaccination.
papers.why: Fatigue illness after infection and after vaccination seems to share the same immune problem. Leftover spike protein together with self-attacking antibodies may drive the illness, whatever the trigger was.

papers.title: Evaluation of an Integrated Multidisciplinary Care Model for Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: A Prospective, Open-label, Non-randomized Controlled Intervention Study
papers.authors: Peters CK (formerly published as Kedor C), Mödl L, Rust R, Stein E, Tietz P, Kim L, Bellmann-Strobl J, Eltity M, Paul F, Veauthier C, Doehner W, Jauert N, Wolfarth B, Thouet T, Mastmeier-Porst J, Reißhauer A, Hoffmann I, Liebl M, Adamaszek M, Erdmann-Reusch B, Stoklossa C, Hagemann A, Steinle E, Kegel L, Grittner U, Konietschke F, Scheibenbogen C, Wittke K
papers.summary: The Charité Fatigue Centrum tested a structured care programme for ME/CFS against usual care with a single visit. The programme included pacing advice, sleep and pain management, nutrition advice, social support and tailored inpatient rehabilitation. 89 patients were in the programme and 93 had usual care, each followed for a year.
papers.why: The extra care did not improve physical function or other key outcomes after a year, and disability got worse in almost half of the programme group. Better-organised care alone does not replace an effective medical treatment.

papers.title: Hemodynamic Phenotyping in ME/CFS and ANOCA: Complementary Insights from Coronary Function Testing and Invasive Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing
papers.authors: Mackay Z, Shah S, Villalobos JG, Latif N, Arun A, Joseph P, Heerdt P, Singh I
papers.journal: American Journal of Physiology-Heart and Circulatory Physiology
papers.summary: 261 people with unexplained chest pain had detailed heart and blood-vessel tests. 18% of them also had ME/CFS, and 89% of these had ANOCA, a condition where the heart's smallest vessels do not work properly although the main arteries look normal. During exercise their hearts delivered oxygen normally, but their muscles had trouble using it, which points to a problem in the muscle.
papers.why: Finding this small-vessel problem changed treatment for 81% of the affected patients. Some chest pain and exercise intolerance in ME/CFS may fit a known, testable heart condition.

papers.title: Clinical Symptomatology, Cognition and Psychosocial Wellbeing in Adolescents With Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: A Cross-Sectional Observational Study
papers.authors: Chau T, Josev EK, Scheinberg A, Thomas N, McDonald F, Reveley C, Gooley PR, Armstrong C, Knight S
papers.journal: Journal of Paediatrics and Child Health
papers.summary: Researchers in Melbourne compared 25 teenagers with mild to moderate ME/CFS with 25 healthy teenagers. Overall intelligence was normal in the ME/CFS group, but they processed information measurably more slowly. They also reported much worse sleep and quality of life and more anxiety and depression. Parents noticed problems with attention and memory.
papers.why: The brain fog young patients describe is a real, measurable slowing of processing speed, not lower intelligence. That supports flexible arrangements at school instead of telling teenagers to try harder.

papers.title: Seven replicated genomic associations of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: a biobank study
papers.authors: Slaughter J, Labayle O, Roskams-Hieter B, Dibble JJ, McGrath SJ, Beentjes SV, Khamseh A, Ponting CP
papers.summary: Researchers used genetic data from the UK Biobank (about 1,268 people with ME/CFS) and checked the results in two smaller groups. Seven gene regions came up again and again. In one of them (CLYBL), the variant linked to ME/CFS goes with lower activity of that gene in brain tissue.
papers.why: The same gene hits now show up outside DecodeME as well. That makes a genetic basis for ME/CFS more likely and gives drug researchers specific genes to look at.

papers.title: Clinical Phenotypes of Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC) Infection: A Longitudinal Cohort Study from Karachi, Pakistan
papers.authors: Khanum I, Ahmed K, Munir T, Zia H, Saif W, Sadia H, Mahmood SF, Nasir N, Ghias K, Rabinowitz P, Van Voorhis W, Iqbal NT
papers.summary: A year-long study in Karachi, Pakistan, followed long-COVID patients' symptoms together with virus remnants in stool samples and serotonin levels in the blood. Most symptoms eased over time, but muscle pain, weakness and fatigue lasted in many. People who still had virus in their stool more often reported breathlessness, fatigue, weakness and joint pain.
papers.why: Rare long-term data from South Asia. It supports two mechanisms proposed for ME/CFS-like fatigue: leftover virus in the gut and disturbed serotonin signalling.

papers.title: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome and overlapping post-acute infection syndromes: international expert consensus framework for diagnostic standardization
papers.authors: Kujawski S, Eaton-Fitch N, Słomko J, Nijs J, Polli A, Hodges L, Morten KJ, Friedman KJ, Hornig M, Djalilian HR, Miglis MG, Godlewska BR, Prusty BK, Bonilla H, Buonsenso D, Tate W, Murovska M, Marshall-Gradisnik S, Zalewski P
papers.summary: 19 international ME/CFS experts agreed on a standard way to measure and score seven core symptoms of ME/CFS and related post-infection illnesses, including long COVID. Among them are post-exertional malaise, problems with automatic body functions such as heart rate or blood pressure, brain fog and sleep problems. They also set out a stepwise testing plan that avoids unnecessary or risky tests.
papers.why: A shared way of measuring symptoms makes studies and drug trials from different centres easier to compare.

papers.title: Fatigue is associated with stimulus-related theta and alpha power and distinguishes subjective from objective cognition in a post-viral cohort: A cross-sectional study
papers.authors: Neumann C, Godbersen L, Schmeer L, et al.
papers.summary: In a large German group of people after viral infections, EEG recordings showed that those who felt more fatigued had different brain-wave patterns (theta and alpha waves) during mental tasks, even when their test results looked normal.
papers.why: An objective marker for a common and puzzling gap in ME/CFS and long COVID: people feel very fatigued although their test performance looks normal.

papers.title: Prevalence and Functional Outcomes of Post-Exertional Malaise among Adults with prior COVID-19: Results from a Representative Survey of New York City Residents
papers.authors: Packard SE, et al.
papers.summary: A survey of more than 9,600 adults in New York City who had had COVID-19 found that about one in five still has post-exertional malaise (PEM), a crash after physical or mental effort. Around 4% have symptoms that have lasted long enough to meet ME/CFS criteria.
papers.why: One of the largest representative estimates of how common PEM is after COVID-19. Women, trans and non-binary people, people of colour, and people with less education or existing disabilities are hit hardest. Doctors should routinely ask about PEM.

papers.title: Total blood volume and red blood cell volume are not associated with orthostatic intolerance in adults with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Yamazaki T, Mancini DM, Blate M, Quan P, Norweg A, Cook DB, Natelson BH
papers.summary: Researchers measured the actual volume of blood and red blood cells in 49 adults with ME/CFS and then tested how they reacted to standing up. More than half had an abnormal standing test, with dizziness, a racing heart or changes in breathing. Whether their blood volume was low, normal or high made no difference.
papers.why: Low blood volume has long been suspected as the cause of standing intolerance in ME/CFS. This study suggests it is not the main cause. Nerves, blood vessels, breathing or brain blood flow look like better treatment targets.

papers.title: Exercise Lactate in Post-COVID-19 Condition: Pathophysiological Signal, Phenotyping Tool, or Candidate Biomarker? A Narrative Review with a Hypothesis-Generating Clinical Observation
papers.authors: Sakellaropoulos SG, Spedicato V, Pfister O
papers.date: Sep 2026 (online ahead of print, print issue Sep 2026)
papers.summary: This review looks at lactate measured during exercise in people with long COVID. Muscles make lactate when they cannot produce energy efficiently. The authors add a small case series of 22 patients whose lactate at peak effort was about six times higher than at rest. They conclude that lactate varies too much between people and test methods to diagnose the condition on its own.
papers.why: Post-exertional malaise is hard to measure objectively. Exercise lactate is an early candidate marker for poor energy metabolism, but the review says it is not ready for clinical use.

papers.title: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome in adolescents with ME/CFS — a case control study
papers.authors: Leone A, Gerrer K, Viereck A, Grabbe A, Kircher A, Behrends U, Maier A
papers.summary: Doctors gave 18 teenagers with ME/CFS and 18 healthy teenagers a simple 10-minute standing test that records heart rate and blood pressure. More than a third of the ME/CFS group had postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), where the heart races too much on standing. None of the healthy teens did. The rise in heart rate during the test alone found POTS almost as well as a specialist examination.
papers.why: A simple, cheap test that any doctor could use to find a treatable circulation problem in teenagers with ME/CFS, which could speed up diagnosis and treatment.

papers.title: A systems microbiology framework for reproducible multi-dataset omics integration with application to long COVID
papers.authors: Varga B, Martinez-Archundia M, Willemsen LEM, Garssen J, Lopez-Rincon A
papers.summary: Researchers built a new computer method to combine several small, inconsistent gene-activity studies of long COVID. They found seven genes for immune response and energy production that showed up across different patient groups, and matched them to existing drugs that might be repurposed.
papers.why: A short list of targets and approved drugs to look at for long COVID, and a method that could find similar signals in ME/CFS.

papers.title: Registered interventional trials fail to cover patient-prioritised treatments in Post-COVID condition (PCC)
papers.authors: Gabriel M, Koster S, Puta C, Katzer K, Reuken PA, Stallmach A
papers.summary: Researchers compared 714 registered post-COVID studies (ClinicalTrials.gov, the German DRKS and the EU registry) with 29 treatments that patients and their doctors actually use. Only about 1 in 14 studies tested any of them. 57 trials measured post-exertional malaise (PEM, the crash after activity), but only 8 used it as the main outcome. Ten common types of treatment had no registered trial at all, for example drugs for nervous-system regulation or mast-cell reactions. The German DRKS registry had no trial of any patient-favoured treatment.
papers.why: Good drug trials that target PEM are rare, and in Germany almost absent. The authors argue that research money, including Germany's new "Nationale Dekade" programme, should also go to the treatments patients and doctors already rely on.

papers.title: A Multivariable Plasma Extracellular Vesicle Surface Profile Associated with Post-COVID-19 Syndrome
papers.authors: Erhart DK, Ressin H, Balz LT, Chatterjee S, Lule D, Mueller S, Lewerenz J, Muench J, Tumani H, Gross RM
papers.summary: The team studied blood and spinal fluid from 61 people with lasting post-COVID symptoms, 80 people who had fully recovered and 10 people with fatigue after other infections. They looked at the proteins on extracellular vesicles (EVs), tiny particles that cells release into the blood. No single protein separated the groups. A computer model that combined many small differences did tell patients and recovered people apart fairly well, and this EV score went down again a year later in patients who got better.
papers.why: This could become a new kind of blood test for post-COVID syndrome. The same Ulm team found no unusual immune activity in these patients' brains, so both results point away from autoimmune brain inflammation as the cause.

papers.title: Auditory sensory gating (P50 suppression) as a biomarker of cognitive fatigue in long COVID
papers.authors: Mischke M, Zaehle T
papers.summary: Researchers measured a brain-wave response called P50 suppression, which shows how well the brain filters out repeated, unimportant sounds, in 71 people with long-COVID fatigue. The worse the filtering, the more mental fatigue people reported, even after taking depression into account.
papers.why: A simple, objective brain-wave measure that tracks mental fatigue independently of mood. It could help build a test for brain fog in long COVID and ME/CFS.

papers.title: Acute Protein Responses Control SARS-CoV-2-specific Neurocognitive and General Post-Viral Sequelae
papers.authors: Liou TG, Andrews RJ, Bass BL, et al. (33 authors, incl. Adler FR)
papers.summary: Saliva samples were taken soon after a COVID-19 infection. People who made more of certain antiviral immune proteins early on were less likely to have lasting brain fog and fatigue months later.
papers.why: A simple early saliva test might one day show who is at risk of long-term post-viral fatigue. The proteins could also be treatment targets.

papers.title: A distinct effector B cell population drives autoantibody production in SARS-CoV-2 infection
papers.authors: Yuan D, Li S, Zhang R, et al.
papers.summary: In blood from COVID-19 patients, researchers found a specific kind of B cell that makes autoantibodies, which attack the body's own tissue. They also identified the signal that switches these cells on.
papers.why: Autoantibodies are a main suspect in ME/CFS and long COVID. Knowing which cells make them and what turns them on gives drug developers a precise target.

papers.title: Plasma Proteomics Identifies a Microtesla Magnetic Therapy Response Signature in Long COVID
papers.authors: Brady NR, Canori A, Maltz D, Kirsher DY, Zhou W, Becker J, Putrino DF, Gurfein BT
papers.summary: In a small trial, people with long-COVID brain fog used a gentle magnetic-field treatment for the whole brain at home ("Microtesla Magnetic Therapy"). Some of them improved. The researchers measured more than 11,000 blood proteins before and after and found about 17 that changed only in the people who got better. One of them normally slows down a signalling pathway (Hedgehog signalling) involved in inflammation and tissue repair, so the treatment may work partly by calming inflammation.
papers.why: A non-drug treatment produced a measurable change in the blood, and some of these proteins might predict who responds. It is a small feasibility study, so the results are early.

papers.title: Early HHV-6 IgG and IgA responses during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection in relation to long COVID: a multicohort observational study
papers.authors: Choudhury A, Burry MJ Jr, Kwon WJ, Yin X, Rallistan A, Presti S, Ndakwah GS, Cheng EQ, Kalaycioglu M, Harris M, Frankovich J, Karlson EW, Bollyky J, Utz PJ, Prestwood TR
papers.summary: Researchers measured antibodies against HHV-6, a common herpes virus that most people carry in a dormant state, in blood taken when people first caught COVID-19. High IgA antibodies against HHV-6 at that point went with a higher chance of later long COVID. High IgG antibodies went with a lower chance.
papers.why: A dormant virus becoming active around the time of infection may help set off long COVID or ME/CFS-like illness. It could also lead to an early blood test for people at risk.

papers.title: Abnormal post-exercise depression of corticomotor excitability is associated with fatigue in post-COVID-19 condition
papers.authors: Sebastianelli L, Dezi S, Ortelli P, Ferrazzoli D, Oliviero A, Versace V
papers.summary: Researchers used magnetic pulses to test the signal from brain to muscle before and after exercise in 58 people with long COVID. The brain's motor output did not recover normally after effort, and this matched how tired patients said they felt.
papers.why: An objective, brain-based way to measure fatigue after exertion, instead of relying only on how tired people say they are. It could help with diagnosis and in trials.

papers.title: Beyond genes: EpiSwitch® and Orion platform-powered 3D genome architecture biomarkers reveal shared biology across ME/CFS, long COVID, PTSD, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis
papers.authors: Hunter E, Alshaker H, Vugrinec D, Bautista S, Gebregzabhar A, Virdi A, Croxford J, Dring A, Powell R, Salter M, Kingdon C, Green J, Akoulitchev A, Pchejetski D
papers.summary: Some genes are switched on or off by how DNA is folded inside the cell, not only by the DNA code. Using a method that reads this folding, researchers compared blood from people with ME/CFS, long COVID, PTSD, rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis. They found folding patterns that these very different illnesses share.
papers.why: These conditions may share some measurable biology. The work extends the same group's earlier ME/CFS blood test (EpiSwitch) to a comparison across diseases that could later help with diagnosis.

papers.title: Cognition-Linked Monocyte State Reveals Altered Myeloid-Lymphoid Coordination in Neuro-PASC
papers.authors: Hanson BA, Cogswell AC, Lopez M, et al.
papers.summary: In older adults with long-COVID brain fog, researchers found certain white blood cells (monocytes) in an unusual state, together with poorer coordination between different parts of the immune system.
papers.why: Faulty immune cells, not only direct brain damage, may be behind fatigue and thinking problems in long COVID and ME/CFS.

papers.title: Micronutrition as a Therapeutic Strategy for Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome and Fibromyalgia: A Narrative Review
papers.authors: Abanades S, Fernandez I, Capdevila N, Cardona F
papers.summary: This review sums up evidence that faulty energy production in the cells (mitochondrial dysfunction) and damage from unstable molecules (oxidative stress) contribute to ME/CFS and fibromyalgia. It asks whether nutrients such as NAD+ precursors, B vitamins, magnesium and CoQ10 could help.
papers.why: A plausible, low-risk approach, but the authors say there is little trial evidence for these supplements in ME/CFS so far and call for proper randomised trials.

papers.title: Nutraceuticals targeting mitochondrial and oxidative-inflammatory pathways for post-exertional malaise and cognitive impairment in long COVID: a narrative review
papers.authors: Praet SFE
papers.summary: This review collects research on cellular energy production (mitochondria), harmful oxygen by-products (oxidative stress) and inflammatory signals. It proposes that certain vitamins, minerals and supplements acting on these pathways could help with crashes after exertion and brain fog in long COVID. None of this has been tested as a treatment.
papers.why: A plan for future supplement trials in long COVID and ME/CFS. It is a review without new patient data, so it does not show that any supplement works.

papers.title: Fragile mitophagy and post-exertional malaise in long COVID: a hypothesis
papers.authors: Groysman R
papers.summary: This paper suggests a new reason why people with long COVID crash one to three days after activity. Damaged mitochondria are marked for clean-up, but the clean-up is not finished. Leftover debris from the mitochondria then keeps inflammation going long after the activity.
papers.why: A new idea for explaining PEM that could be tested with existing lab methods. It is a single author's hypothesis without new data.

papers.title: Acupressure and Qigong in post-infectious fatigue with impaired physical function: a randomized clinical trial
papers.authors: Dietzel J, Bauer T, Tissen-Diabaté T, Ortiz M, Siewert J, Bellmann-Strobl J, Engelhardt U, Roll S, Grabowska W, Scheibenbogen C, Willich SN, Paul F, Brinkhaus B
papers.summary: In this Charité trial (ACUQiG), 235 people with lasting fatigue and reduced physical function after an infection, mostly COVID-19, were split into two groups. One group pressed on specific body points every day for about 18 minutes (acupressure) and did online Qigong, a gentle movement practice, twice a week for 8 weeks. The other group got a self-care leaflet. Physical function, the main outcome, was only slightly better in the acupressure group, and the difference could have been chance. Fatigue improved a little, and that effect was statistically real.
papers.why: A careful trial from Carmen Scheibenbogen's group at Charité. It missed its main goal, so expectations for this kind of approach should stay modest, even though fatigue improved slightly.

papers.title: Voluntary wheel running behavior is reduced by SARS-CoV-2 S1 administration and mitigates hypothalamic neuroinflammatory processes
papers.authors: Kelley T, Frank MG, Ball JB, Hopkins S, Nguyen TH, Thompson RS, Maier SF, Fleshner M
papers.summary: In rats, injecting part of the coronavirus spike protein into the brain fluid made the animals run less on their own, which researchers use as a sign of fatigue. Letting the rats run voluntarily reduced the brain inflammation the spike protein had caused.
papers.why: An animal model linking a virus protein to brain inflammation and less activity. In this model some exercise calmed the inflammation, which contrasts with reports that exertion harms people with ME/CFS.

papers.title: eNOS Uncoupling, Shear-Stress Tolerance, and the Two-Threshold Model of Post-Exertional Malaise in Long COVID: A Mechanistic Hypothesis With Implications for Physiotherapy and Recovery Protocols
papers.authors: Karipidis YK, Karipidis KY
papers.summary: This is a theory paper without new patient data. It deals with long-COVID patients who get post-exertional malaise (PEM) even though their blood vessels look normal on standard scans. The authors think COVID-19 damages the inner lining of the vessels and uses up a helper molecule needed to make nitric oxide, a gas that lets vessels widen during activity. Without it, the same enzyme makes harmful by-products instead. These would build up during and after exertion and cause the crash.
papers.why: It is a blood-vessel explanation for PEM that can be tested with blood samples taken before and after exercise. It differs from Klaus Wirth's muscle-calcium theory. The authors also suggest that too much rest could harm vessel function, which matters for pacing advice.

papers.title: REenergizeME: intermittent hypoxia-hyperoxia treatment for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome — protocol for a randomised, placebo-controlled trial
papers.authors: Nochi M, Kristensen SK, Mehrani N, Guerreiro I, Nørholm IMD, Chandra S, Olufsen M, Gudbergsen LR, Brinth LS, Stokholm R, Karlsson P, Tankisi H, Mehlsen J, Foldager CB, Olsen RKJ
papers.summary: This is a study plan, so there are no results yet. A Danish trial will test intermittent hypoxia-hyperoxia treatment (IHHT) in 104 adults with ME/CFS. Patients breathe air with less oxygen, then more oxygen than normal, in short repeated cycles. The aim is to retrain how cells make energy.
papers.why: It is a non-drug treatment aimed at one suspected cause of fatigue: cells that handle oxygen and energy poorly. Quality of life and post-exertional malaise are key outcomes. Results are still to come.

papers.title: Data-driven subtypes of internalizing and functional somatic symptoms: A hybrid mixture modeling approach
papers.authors: Saini U, Wanders R, Oldehinkel AJ, Rosmalen JGM, van Loo HM
papers.summary: The researchers used survey data from almost 73,000 adults in the Netherlands. They grouped people by their symptoms, not by diagnosis, and looked at depression, anxiety, ME/CFS, fibromyalgia and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) together. In one group, defined mainly by brain fog and fatigue, ME/CFS symptoms overlapped a lot with depression and anxiety symptoms. Pain symptoms formed a separate group.
papers.why: Part of the overlap between ME/CFS and mood disorders may come from shared, unspecific symptoms like fatigue and poor concentration. It does not mean they are the same illness. Objective biomarkers are needed to tell them apart.

papers.title: Experimental hypoxia to probe neuro-metabolic and vascular dysregulation in ME/CFS: a multimodal proof-of-concept MRI study
papers.authors: Bader V, Estermann K, Niess E, Zrzavy T, Fischmeister F, Haider T, Ludwig B, Barkhof F, Mutsaerts H, Kasprian G, Niess F, Bogner W, Kollndorfer K, Haider L
papers.summary: 26 people with ME/CFS and 27 healthy people had MRI brain scans while breathing normal air and then air with a little less oxygen. The patients' brains contained more lactate even before the oxygen was lowered. Lactate builds up when energy is made without enough oxygen. Their brain blood flow also reacted to low oxygen much less evenly than in healthy people, and their brainstem was slightly smaller.
papers.why: Brain scans support the idea that cells in ME/CFS struggle to make energy and that blood flow does not adjust normally under strain. Some of these scan measures could become objective tests in future trials.

papers.title: Cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure in relation to symptomatology and craniocervical anatomy in patients with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Jolley C, Bragée B, Soinne L, Huhmar H, Billing H, Bertilson B, Sjögren P
papers.summary: 34 ME/CFS patients had a lumbar puncture, a needle test that measures fluid pressure around the brain and spinal cord. Just over a third had higher pressure than normal. These patients were much more likely to feel better in the days after the test, which lowers the pressure for a while.
papers.why: There may be a subgroup with raised fluid pressure that could be treated. A simple pressure measurement could show who might benefit from pressure-lowering treatment.

papers.title: Persistent Neurological Symptoms After COVID-19 Lack Evidence of Adaptive CNS Immune Activation
papers.authors: Erhart DK, Balz LT, Giotaki I, Matits L, Gross R, Bachhuber F, Muench J, Kolassa I, Fitzner D, Uttner I, Lule D, Lewerenz J, Lange P, Tumani H
papers.summary: Spinal-fluid tests in 50 people with ongoing post-COVID brain fog and fatigue were compared with 50 people who had fully recovered. The patients showed no extra immune activity in the brain and no self-attacking antibodies, although their memory and fatigue were clearly worse.
papers.why: This speaks against ongoing brain inflammation or autoimmunity as the main cause of lasting neurological post-COVID symptoms. Other explanations, such as metabolic or blood-vessel changes, become more likely.

papers.title: Perivascular spaces in neuropsychiatric post-COVID syndrome
papers.authors: Bernal J, Ilik SY, Mai H, Mattern H, Coello RD, Valdés-Hernández Md, Rocktäschel T, Reuken PA, Stallmach A, Wardlaw J, Opel N, Gaser C, Walter M, Ziegler G, Düzel E, Schreiber S, Besteher B
papers.summary: Brain scans of 116 people, 59 with lasting post-COVID brain fog or fatigue and 57 without, looked at the small fluid channels around brain blood vessels (perivascular spaces). They are part of the brain's waste-clearance system. Older patients and those who had been ill longer had more enlarged channels, and this went with worse physical function.
papers.why: A visible scan marker that fits other findings about blood vessels and fluid drainage in the brain in ME/CFS-like illness.

papers.title: Haptoglobin Phenotypes Stratify Post-Exertional Cognitive Dysfunction Associated with Altered Cerebral Oxygenation and Metabolic Signatures in Long COVID
papers.authors: Moezzi A, Elremaly W, Leveau C, Franco A, Nepotchatykh O, Armstrong CW, Moreau A
papers.summary: Haptoglobin is a blood protein that comes in different inherited forms. Researchers gave 44 long-COVID patients and 20 recovered people a 90-minute exertion challenge. People with the Hp2-2 form scored clearly worse on thinking tests afterwards and showed differences in brain oxygen and blood chemistry. People with the Hp1-1 form stayed stable.
papers.why: A simple genetic test might explain why some people get much worse brain fog after exertion than others. The same team found this earlier in ME/CFS. It could help identify who needs the most protection from overexertion.

papers.title: Identifying EEG biomarkers of fatigue and brain fog in long COVID: insights from rest and movement-related brain activity
papers.authors: Casado Sánchez M, Morales Fajardo K, Long S, Janaudis-Ferreira T, Duclos C, Boudrias MH
papers.summary: Researchers recorded brain activity with an EEG cap in 20 people with long COVID and 20 healthy people, at rest and during a hand-grip task. The patients' brain activity bounced back less after movement, and their resting rhythm over the movement area was slower. Both went with fatigue and brain fog.
papers.why: Brain fog is hard to measure or prove. These two EEG signals could become objective tests for it and show whether treatments work.

papers.title: Impact of immunoadsorption on autoantibodies and physical performance in post-COVID patients: a prospective exploratory study of 18 participants
papers.authors: Wossidlo C, Steinbeck F, Geerdes-Fenge H, Sombetzki M, Mitzner S, Loebermann M, Reisinger EC, Koball S
papers.summary: Immunoadsorption filters antibodies out of the blood. 18 post-COVID patients with raised antibodies against their own stress-hormone receptors were treated. Antibody levels dropped clearly but came back within 3 to 6 months. Performance in objective physical tests did not improve. Pain and fatigue improved only slightly, by the patients' own report.
papers.why: A mostly negative result from a German university group outside Charité, about the same approach used in Scheibenbogen's immunoadsorption studies. Removing these antibodies may not be enough on its own.

papers.title: Long-term angiogenic and thromboinflammatory signatures in post-COVID-19 syndrome
papers.authors: Mora Zetina AA, Ortega Sanchez EF, Zuñiga Ascencio BS, Castorena Maldonado AR, Ahumada Topete VH, Torres Espíndola LM, Aquino Gálvez A, et al.
papers.summary: Researchers checked 32 people three and a half years after a hospital stay for COVID-19. About two thirds still had fatigue, breathlessness or trouble concentrating. Their blood still showed high levels of proteins that drive blood-vessel growth (VEGF-D, angiopoietin-1) and signs of a sluggish clotting system.
papers.why: Blood-vessel and clotting changes can last for years after COVID-19. The same idea, including microclots, is behind some treatment approaches in ME/CFS.

papers.title: Multiomic and Spatial Profiling of Colorectal Tissue Reveals Viral Persistence and Immune Dysregulation in Long COVID
papers.authors: LaFranchi B, Maison DP, Vinden J, Rodriguez AE, Tout A, Grimbert L, et al., Peluso MJ, Henrich TJ
papers.summary: Gut tissue and blood from 44 people with long COVID were compared with 13 people who had fully recovered. Pieces of the coronavirus were still sitting in the gut lining of the patients. Immune cells nearby kept up an inflammation but failed to clear the virus.
papers.why: This supports the idea that leftover virus keeps the immune system busy. The idea is also discussed for ME/CFS and is the reason for antiviral and immune-based trials.

papers.title: Peripheral metabolic signatures in patients with neuropsychiatric long COVID syndrome
papers.authors: Bergmann DL, Neugebauer S, Rocktäschel T, Dommaschk EM, Li M, Weuthen A, Refisch A, Blekic N, Kiehntopf M, Scherag A, Schiöth HB, Lim CK, Opel N, Walter M, Besteher B
papers.summary: Long-COVID patients with brain fog, low mood and similar symptoms had unusual blood levels of fats the body uses to store and move energy (triglycerides and acylcarnitines). The more severe their fatigue and depression, the larger these changes, and they matched differences on brain scans.
papers.why: A disturbed fat and energy metabolism, similar to the energy problems proposed for ME/CFS, may drive the fatigue. It could be a target for metabolic treatments.

papers.title: Virus reactivation in acute and long COVID-19
papers.authors: Maguire C, Chen J, Rouphael N, and the IMPACC Network (180+ contributors, incl. Baden LR, Simon V, Davis MM, Nadeau KC, Krammer F)
papers.summary: In more than a thousand people in hospital with COVID-19, dormant viruses that many people carry, such as Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus, often became active again during severe illness. This happened even when the rest of the immune system worked normally. Usually harmless anelloviruses also became active. Unlike the herpesviruses, they stayed active for months, and this was linked to developing long COVID.
papers.why: A large study supporting one leading theory: viruses that wake up again keep the immune system on alert long after the infection. Antiviral and immune treatments tested in ME/CFS are based on the same idea.

papers.title: Feasibility and outcomes of crossflow membrane plasmapheresis for long COVID in Suriname: a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled pilot trial
papers.authors: Bihariesingh-Sanchit R, Bansie R, Paltoe P, Ma R, Bustamente D, Ramesar D, Raghosing-Sanchit R, Codrington J, Ma-Bihariesingh I, Vreden S, van der Dijs F, Mangroo R, Simson M, Ramdhani N, Fung A Foek C, van 't Wout A, Diavatopoulos D, de Jonge M, Nierich A
papers.summary: In a small pilot study in Suriname, 18 people with long COVID got either real plasma exchange (part of the blood plasma is filtered and replaced, over 5 sessions) or a sham procedure, decided by chance. Three months later the real-treatment group reported clearly less fatigue and the sham group did not. The study was too small to prove a real difference. There were no serious side effects.
papers.why: Early and inconclusive evidence that filtering blood plasma may help with long-COVID fatigue. It is related to the immunoadsorption studies by Scheibenbogen's group, and the authors call for a larger trial.

papers.title: The Mammillary Body-Fornix Gate in Long COVID: An exploratory structural and diffusion MRI study of tremor-like symptoms, internal vibrations, and neuromuscular fatigue
papers.authors: Ziaja CP, Young SY, Stark MS, Zurek G, Sedlacik J, Wright FM
papers.summary: MRI scans, including a method that maps the brain's wiring, compared 88 long-COVID patients who had tremor, a feeling of inner vibration and severe fatigue with 34 healthy people. The patients showed differences in the mammillary bodies, a small pair of structures deep in the brain involved in memory and passing on body signals. The nerve tracts connected to them and the cerebellum, which coordinates movement, were also changed.
papers.why: This suggests a physical cause in the brain for unusual tremor and vibration symptoms that some patients report. It is a small, early study that has not been peer-reviewed yet.

papers.title: A cardiometabolic perspective on post-exertional malaise in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) and Long COVID
papers.authors: Westermeier F, Pretorius E, Untersmayr E, Bertinat R, Sepúlveda N, Fisman E
papers.summary: This opinion paper argues that post-exertional malaise (PEM), the crash after activity, is not one system flaring up. It is a breakdown in how the heart, blood vessels and metabolism work together in the hours and days after exertion, especially in people who also have obesity or type 2 diabetes.
papers.why: It suggests studying PEM by following the heart and metabolism together over time after exertion, which could help design better drug trials for PEM.

papers.title: Microvascular remodeling and endothelial dysfunction across the post-COVID-19 spectrum: a prospective observational case-control study
papers.authors: Wallraven T, Günthner R, Lethen I, Ribeiro A, Lech M, Oertel FC, Reeß LG, Haller B, Streese L, Hanssen H, Basta-Wunderle M, Schmaderer C
papers.summary: A special camera watched how the tiny blood vessels at the back of the eye react to flickering light. The study included 96 healthy people, 102 people fully recovered from COVID-19 and 102 people with lasting post-COVID symptoms, 62 of whom met full ME/CFS criteria. The patients' vessels widened less and were narrower at rest. This was worst in the ME/CFS group, whose blood also showed more markers of inflamed, damaged vessel walls.
papers.why: A simple, non-invasive eye test could detect and measure the blood-vessel problems in ME/CFS, help with earlier diagnosis and show whether vessel-targeted treatments work.

papers.title: Persistent Hypercoagulability and Further Characterization of Microclot Complexes in Long COVID
papers.authors: Nunes M, Pereira Guerreiro CM, Pretorius JH, Venter C, Thierry AR, Fielding BC, Kell DB, Pretorius E
papers.summary: Blood from 20 people with long COVID and 19 healthy people was tested. The patients' blood clotted faster and more firmly than normal (hypercoagulability) and contained more microclots, small clumps of misfolded blood protein that special dyes can stain.
papers.why: From Etheresia Pretorius's group, the lab best known for this work. More detailed support for the microclot theory: hard-to-dissolve clots may block small vessels and starve tissue of oxygen.

papers.title: Persistent Mitochondrial and Endothelial Dysfunction in Non-Hospitalized Patients with Long COVID
papers.authors: Ono R, Takayama S, Abe M, Arita R, Onodera K, Ishizawa K, Kanno T, Saito N, Kikuchi A, Abe T, Ishii T
papers.summary: 32 people with long COVID in Japan were followed for 6 months. Two blood markers, one for stress in the mitochondria and one for damage to the blood-vessel lining, stayed high in patients who did not improve and fell in those who did. 91% of the participants had fatigue as a main symptom.
papers.why: The authors think the same mitochondrial and blood-vessel problems probably underlie fatigue in ME/CFS. The markers could serve as a simple blood test to see who stays ill.

papers.title: Circulating MicroRNA ratios as diagnostic biomarkers for long COVID with an independent validation cohort
papers.authors: Han E, Lukovic D, Müller-Zlabinger K, Hasimbegovic E, Schefberger K, Kastner N, Spannbauer A, Riesenhuber M, Nitsche C, Zelniker TA, Gyöngyösi M, Hamzaraj K
papers.summary: Researchers at the Medical University of Vienna tested blood from 206 long-COVID patients and 71 healthy people for ratios of microRNAs, tiny genetic messengers linked to mitochondria and blood vessels. Two ratios were reliably lower in patients in two separate groups. Accuracy dropped when the test was checked against outside data.
papers.why: A step towards an objective blood test for long COVID that might also work for ME/CFS. The authors say it is not accurate enough for clinical use yet.

papers.title: EBV Reprograms B Cells in an Autoimmune-Like Fashion in Patients with COVID-19
papers.authors: Chen DG, Yuan D, Su Y, Magis A, Chu H, Goldman JD, Heath JR
papers.summary: In COVID-19 patients, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a dormant virus most people carry, can wake up and reprogram the B cells it infects so that they act as if they were attacking the body's own tissue. People with more of these reprogrammed cells had worse lingering symptoms 2 to 3 months later.
papers.why: EBV has long been suspected in long COVID and ME/CFS. This study shows a specific way a reawakened virus could drive lasting illness.

papers.title: Orthostatic Dysfunction and Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: A Close Reciprocal Relationship Beyond Cardiac Preload Failure and Hypoperfusion
papers.authors: Wirth KJ
papers.summary: Standing up puts extra strain on the body, and many people with ME/CFS feel worse when upright (orthostatic intolerance). This paper argues that standing does more than strain the heart and vessels. It may also overload muscle cells with calcium, the same process Klaus Wirth believes causes post-exertional malaise.
papers.why: Wirth's own hypothesis that standing alone could trigger crashes in severely ill patients through the same mechanism as exertion. It links two of the most disabling symptoms and still needs supporting data.

papers.title: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for the treatment of long COVID (RECOVER-VITAL): a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial
papers.authors: Baden LR, Shah NS, Liu STH, Cohen J, Moy J, Kumar A, McComsey GA, Chen P, Floris-Moore M, Singer NG, Fernandez I, Slandzicki AJ, Wiley Z, Kadl A, Kaminsky DA, Hsu H, Walker TA, Hope AA, Ostrosky-Zeichner L, Goldman JD, Peluso MJ, Patterson TF, Parthasarathy S, Mullington JM, et al., for the RECOVER-VITAL Clinical Trial Group
papers.summary: In this large US trial, 959 adults who had had long-COVID symptoms for at least 12 weeks were randomly given the antiviral Paxlovid (nirmatrelvir-ritonavir) or a placebo for 15 or 25 days. The aim was to test whether hidden virus drives the symptoms. The drug was no better than placebo on any measure, whether people mainly had brain fog, dizziness and a fast heart rate, or exercise intolerance.
papers.why: The largest and most careful test so far of the idea that leftover virus causes long COVID. It found no benefit. Research now turns to other explanations, including for the form with crashes after exertion that overlaps with ME/CFS.

papers.title: Gut microbiome signatures during acute infection are associated with long COVID
papers.authors: Comba IY, Mars RAT, Yang L, Dumais M, Chen J, Van Gorp TM, et al.
papers.summary: People were followed from their first COVID-19 infection onwards. The mix of gut bacteria during the acute illness, not later, predicted who would develop long COVID. Different bacterial patterns went with different symptom patterns.
papers.why: A gut-bacteria test during the first infection might one day show who is at risk of long COVID. The link between gut and immune system could be an early treatment target.

papers.title: The Post-COVID syndrome caused by excessive inflammation: pathogenesis, potential targets and therapeutic agents
papers.authors: Zhou T, Xue G, Zhang Y, Li M, Zhang D, Lin J, Luo C, Han L, Tian J, Huang H
papers.summary: A review of the evidence that ongoing, excessive inflammation drives long-COVID fatigue, with a list of drugs and other treatments being explored to calm it.
papers.why: A list of anti-inflammatory drug candidates that future long-COVID and ME/CFS trials could test.

papers.title: Uncovering the hidden biology of fibrinaloid microclot complexes in complex, inflammatory diseases
papers.authors: Grixti J, Pretorius E, Kell DB
papers.summary: Microclots are unusually tough blood clots that are hard to dissolve. Some researchers think they build up in inflammatory illnesses. This review from a leading microclot group explains how they form, why the body has trouble breaking them down and how they might cause symptoms in ME/CFS and long COVID.
papers.why: From Etheresia Pretorius and Douglas Kell, the group best known for this work. It summarises and extends the microclot and blood-vessel theory behind some treatment ideas in ME/CFS and long COVID.

papers.title: VSL#3® supplementation improves fatigue in long COVID: results from the DELong#3 randomized placebo-controlled trial
papers.authors: Amoroso C, Marinoni B, Maragno P, Rimondi A, Bottaro F, Ciafardini C, Muià M, Honcharyuk I, Noviello D, Caridi B, Sommella EM, Bandera A, Gori A, Mantero M, Blasi F, Ferrucci R, Priori A, Strati F, Vecchi M, Facciotti F, Caprioli F
papers.summary: In this Italian trial (DELong#3), 48 adults with lasting fatigue after COVID-19 took either a high-dose probiotic with several bacterial strains (VSL#3) or a placebo for four weeks. Fatigue dropped much more with the probiotic, and the improvement was still there a month after they stopped.
papers.why: One of the few placebo-controlled trials that found less fatigue in long COVID. It points to the gut bacteria as a low-risk treatment target. The trial was small and needs to be repeated with more people.

papers.title: Subclinical neurovascular and immune correlates of post-COVID-19 syndrome detected by retinal imaging
papers.authors: Wunderle M, Wicklein R, Ribeiro A, Carbajo-Lozoya J, Wöhnl A, Negele J, et al.
papers.summary: Detailed eye imaging found small changes in the tiny blood vessels and in immune activity at the back of the eye in people with post-COVID syndrome, even when standard eye exams were normal.
papers.why: The retina is one of the few places where doctors can look directly at small vessels and nerve tissue. These changes give a non-invasive view of vessel and immune problems that may underlie fatigue after COVID and in ME/CFS.

papers.title: Small extracellular vesicles proteome reveals persistent inflammatory and coagulopathic dysregulation in long-COVID
papers.authors: Chandran S, Chen L, Ram AK, Spikes L, Chalise P, Dhillon NK
papers.summary: In long-COVID patients with fatigue, brain fog and sleep problems, the proteins carried by tiny blood particles (extracellular vesicles) showed lasting signs of inflammation and abnormal clotting.
papers.why: Another lab with another method finds inflammation and abnormal clotting in long COVID, the same area as the microclot research.

papers.title: Associations between multidimensional fatigue and wearable-derived cardio-respiratory variables in post-COVID-19 patients: an observational study
papers.authors: Adão Martins NR, Annaheim S, Büche D, Rossi RM, Spengler CM
papers.summary: 30 people in post-COVID rehabilitation wore sensors day and night that recorded heart rate and breathing. Physical, mental and emotional tiredness each matched a different pattern in these signals.
papers.why: Wrist or chest sensors could track different kinds of fatigue over time. That helps with pacing and with measuring whether treatments work.

papers.title: Symptom-based clusters in people with post-COVID-19 condition (PCC)
papers.authors: Kuczyk C, Herrmann-Lingen C, Stolz M, Krauth C, Burger B, Stahmeyer JT, Nöhre M, Debener A, Käufer C, Richter F, Derad C, Hellmich M, de Zwaan M
papers.summary: In 1,673 people with post-COVID condition in Germany, researchers grouped patients by their pattern of 14 symptoms, including fatigue, instead of using one label. They found distinct subgroups that differed in age, sex and psychological factors.
papers.why: A large German study showing that post-COVID condition is not one illness but several subgroups. That matters for tailoring treatment and for who German trials include.

papers.title: Loss of vesicular monoamine transporter 2 in striatum of long COVID and relationship to neuropsychiatric symptoms
papers.authors: Liu YK, Persaud D, Vieira EL, et al.
papers.summary: Brain scans of people with long COVID showed fewer working dopamine-releasing nerve endings in a region for motivation and movement. The bigger the loss, the more apathetic, slowed down or forgetful people felt.
papers.why: A measurable brain change behind some motivation and thinking problems in long COVID. Treatments that boost dopamine signalling could be tested.

papers.title: Chronic Stress Primes TLR3-Mediated Systemic Inflammation to Produce Persistent Post-Viral Fatigue Syndrome-Like Symptoms in Mice
papers.authors: Lkhagvasuren B, Suematsu T, Xiangyu L, Hata T, Takakura S, Hiramoto T, Oka T, Sudo N
papers.summary: Mice that were stressed for a long time and then given a molecule that mimics a viral infection developed lasting fatigue, pain sensitivity, memory problems and less social behaviour, similar to post-viral fatigue syndrome. Minocycline, a drug that calms overactive immune cells in the brain, partly reversed these effects.
papers.why: In a controlled animal model, stress followed by a virus-like immune trigger caused lasting ME/CFS-like symptoms through brain inflammation, and calming that inflammation partly undid them. This supports brain inflammation as a treatable driver of post-viral fatigue.

papers.title: Cognitive rehabilitation for adults with long COVID: a randomized clinical trial
papers.authors: Vanova M, Patel AMR, Scott I, Gilpin G, Manning EN, Ash C, Wittenberg P, Lim J, Hoare Z, Evans R, Bray N, Kipps CM, Devine C, Ahmed S, Dunne R, Koniotes A, Warren C, Chan D, Suarez-Gonzalez A
papers.summary: In a trial in England, 78 adults with lasting brain fog after COVID-19 were randomly assigned to ten weekly one-to-one sessions of cognitive rehabilitation or to usual care. The sessions were practical coaching on everyday goals they chose themselves, such as remembering appointments. The coaching group made clearly more progress on their goals, and much of the benefit lasted six months.
papers.why: A well-designed randomised trial showing that a non-drug treatment can help with long-COVID brain fog, for which there is no approved treatment.

papers.title: Skeletal muscle properties in long COVID and ME/CFS differ from those induced by bed rest
papers.authors: Charlton BT, Slaghekke A, Appelman B, Eggelbusch M, Huijts JY, Noort W, Hendrickse PW, Bloemers FW, Posthuma JJ, van Amstel P, Goulding RP, Degens H, Jaspers RT, van Vugt M, Wüst RCI
papers.summary: Researchers compared muscle samples and exercise tests from people with long COVID and ME/CFS with healthy volunteers who had spent 60 days in strict bed rest, a standard way to mimic deconditioning. Patients had fewer small blood vessels in their muscles and more fast fibres that tire quickly. Bed rest does not produce this pattern. People with ME/CFS had also lost some of their slow, fatigue-resistant fibres.
papers.why: The muscle changes are not explained by inactivity alone. They point to a real disease process in the muscle, which fits Klaus Wirth's muscle theory of post-exertional malaise, although he was not involved in this study.

papers.title: Orthostatic intolerance with small heart and/or disequilibrium in patients with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: clinical update and paradigm shift
papers.authors: Miwa K
papers.summary: This review argues that dizziness and fatigue when standing in ME/CFS often have two overlooked causes. One is an unusually small heart that pumps less blood. The other is a subtle problem in the balance system of the inner ear and brain. Blood pooling in the legs is only part of the story.
papers.why: It names concrete, testable causes for a disabling symptom. That points to other treatment targets, such as the heart's output or the balance system, than standard care for orthostatic intolerance.

papers.title: Association between myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome and irritable bowel syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Rajabi N, Ramdass PVAK
papers.summary: Pooling 22 studies, people with ME/CFS were about seven times more likely to also have irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) than people without ME/CFS. Roughly 1 in 3 people with ME/CFS also has IBS.
papers.why: The overlap is large and consistent. It suggests shared biology in the immune system, nerves and gut signalling, and argues for treating gut and fatigue symptoms together instead of separately.

papers.title: ADDRESS-LC: study protocol for a phase 2, triple-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy and safety of bezisterim (NE3107) in adults with long COVID
papers.authors: Markham P, Peluso MJ, Hsiang-Yi Chou S, McCorkell L, O'Quinn S, Reading C, Ahlem C, Petit CM, Yan J, Palumbo JM
papers.summary: This is a study plan, so no results yet. The trial will test bezisterim, a drug that dampens one inflammation pathway in body and brain, in 208 adults who have had long-COVID fatigue and brain fog for at least three months. Half get the drug and half a placebo for 12 weeks. Neither patients nor doctors know who gets what.
papers.why: The trial tests whether ongoing brain inflammation drives long-COVID fatigue and brain fog, using a drug already tried in other inflammatory brain conditions. Results are still to come.

papers.title: Central origin of fatigability in Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome revealed by multimodal neuroimaging
papers.authors: Bedard P, Knutson KM, McGurrin PM, Vial F, Popa T, Horovitz SG, Hallett M, Nath A, Walitt B
papers.summary: In a hand-grip test, people with ME/CFS reached the same maximum strength as healthy people but tired much sooner. Recordings of brain and muscle activity showed that healthy people's brain signals rose as they tired, to make up for it. In ME/CFS this brain signal hardly rose at all.
papers.why: Part of the fatigue in ME/CFS seems to come from how the brain drives tired muscles. Treatments for exhaustion and crashes may need to target the nervous system too.

papers.title: The role of disease history score in the association between depression history and current myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Mao S, Wu L
papers.summary: Using survey data from more than 10,000 US adults, researchers found that people with past depression were more likely to have ME/CFS now. Much of this link was explained by a wider history of past illnesses and health problems (a combined disease-history score). The link was stronger in women and older adults.
papers.why: Depression probably does not simply cause ME/CFS. Both may reflect a person's overall history of illness, so ME/CFS should be judged in that full context and not reduced to a psychiatric diagnosis.

papers.title: Associated factors and a risk prediction model for comorbid circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome: implications for early screening and sleep health management
papers.authors: Shao X, Yang F, Qin LL, Shi JN, Chen M, Ge WJ, Jiang TJ, Yue JW, Feng W, Wang JH, Zhang ZX
papers.summary: In a hospital study in China with 610 people with chronic fatigue syndrome, almost half also had a circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder, meaning the body clock is out of step with normal sleeping and waking times. The researchers built a simple score from shift work, fatigue severity, female sex and reduced deep sleep to predict who has it.
papers.why: Doctors could use the score to find patients with a treatable sleep-timing problem. The data come from one hospital, and it is unclear whether international ME/CFS criteria were used.

papers.title: Circulating extracellular vesicles-microRNAs as potential biomarkers for the identification of ME/CFS: differentiating fatigue-related conditions
papers.authors: Eguchi A, Kuratsune H, Nakatomi Y, Yasui T, Nakagawa R, Watanabe Y, Fukuda S
papers.summary: Researchers compared tiny particles released by cells into the blood (extracellular vesicles) and the small RNA pieces they carry (microRNAs) in people with ME/CFS, people with ordinary chronic fatigue and people with depression. ME/CFS patients had their own pattern of particles and about 62 microRNAs that differed from the other groups. These point to changes in nerve cells and cell structure.
papers.why: One more candidate for a blood test that could separate ME/CFS from depression or general tiredness, which no test can do reliably today. The study is small and needs to be repeated.

papers.title: Multimodal approach to identify neuropsychophysiological subgroups in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome and their relevance for rehabilitation
papers.authors: Dooms Y, Qiu L, Coppieters I, Vergaelen E, Claes S, Dupont P, Hehl M, Cuypers K, Engler H, Dombrowski K, Verbeke K, Van den Bergh O, Raes J, Van Oudenhove L, Van Den Houte M, Bogaerts K
papers.summary: This is a study plan, so no results yet. A Belgian study will examine 115 people with ME/CFS and 55 healthy people with many tests: inflammation markers, brain scans for inflammation, nervous-system function, gut bacteria and stress hormones. Patients will then go through a rehabilitation programme to see which measurements predict who improves.
papers.why: The goal is to sort patients into biological subgroups so treatment, including rehabilitation, can match what drives each person's illness. Results are still to come.

papers.title: Agreement and reliability between the two-day 6-minute incremental step test and two-day cardiopulmonary exercise test in post COVID-19 condition for assessing post-exertional malaise: The REVEAL-study
papers.authors: Bomans S, Michotte N, El M'Rabet I, Jimenez Garcia B, Leemans L, Janssens P, Hanon S, De Waele E, Beckwée D
papers.summary: Researchers checked whether a simpler 6-minute step test, done on two days, could replace the demanding two-day cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET, a bike or treadmill test that measures oxygen use) for detecting post-exertional malaise in 25 people with post-COVID condition. The step test agreed only partly with CPET, especially on oxygen use and muscle symptoms. It is not reliable enough yet to replace it.
papers.why: An easier way to measure PEM would make drug trials much simpler to run. This study shows the simple test still needs work.

papers.title: Microstructural alterations in brain tissue of ME/CFS and long COVID using diffusion tensor imaging and diffusion kurtosis imaging
papers.authors: Singh TB, Marshall-Gradisnik S, Barnden L, Eaton-Fitch N, Huynh TH, Inderyas M, Thapaliya K
papers.summary: Two advanced MRI methods that map the fine fibres between brain regions were used to compare 37 people with ME/CFS, 19 with long COVID and 27 healthy people. Both patient groups differed from healthy people, but in different areas and in different ways. Examples are a region for planning movement and the fibre bundle that links the two halves of the brain.
papers.why: One of the first direct comparisons of brain wiring in ME/CFS and long COVID. The two illnesses may need to be studied and treated as biologically different.

papers.title: Handgrip strength in children, adolescents, and young adults with suspected myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Mihatsch L, Schartner L, de Luna JL, Höhler C, Bucka L, Lovrenovic L, Eidenschink S, Schmuck B, Bienemann V, Christa C, Mittelstraß K, Hausruckinger A, Warlitz C, Michel K, Gerrer K, Freitag H, Scheibenbogen C, Pricoco R, Behrends U
papers.summary: Researchers measured grip strength twice, an hour apart, in 147 young people aged 10 to 25 who were being assessed for ME/CFS, and in 83 healthy peers. The patients' grip strength, and how it changed between the two tests, differed from the healthy group. On its own, the test could not reliably separate ME/CFS from other conditions that cause tiredness.
papers.why: From Carmen Scheibenbogen's group. A simple, cheap test that could track muscle weakness after exertion in children and teenagers in future drug trials, even though it cannot diagnose ME/CFS by itself.

papers.title: Association of rapamycin treatment with the modulation of purine metabolism, reduced microglial inflammatory responses, improved mitochondrial energy metabolism, and alleviation of fatigue symptoms in ME/CFS subjects: pilot findings from phase-II observational study
papers.authors: Gile B, Bulbule S, Toriola MA, Ruan BT, Marium S, Benko A, Grach S, Mueller M, Bateman L, Bell J, Yellman B, Berner J, Chheda B, Kaufman D, Gottschalk G, Roy A
papers.summary: In a small ongoing study without a placebo group, people with ME/CFS took low-dose rapamycin for three months. Rapamycin dampens an overactive cell-growth signal. Blood and immune tests showed changes in energy-related substances, calmer immune cells in the brain and better-working mitochondria. Patients reported less fatigue.
papers.why: Few ME/CFS drug studies show changes in measurable body chemistry together with fewer symptoms. That gives a biological reason to keep testing rapamycin, ideally against a placebo.

papers.title: Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS) gene expression signatures for the identification of compounds targeting metabolism
papers.authors: Dehlia A, Alizada Z, Guthridge MA
papers.summary: Researchers combined two sets of gene-activity data from ME/CFS patients and found 46 genes that behave differently. A computer search then looked for existing drugs that might reverse this pattern. Three of four candidates, including the approved diabetes drug pioglitazone, slightly increased energy production in muscle cells grown in the lab.
papers.why: Approved drugs that act on cellular energy could be tested in ME/CFS faster than new ones. The computer analysis also fits the idea that energy production is disturbed.

papers.title: Perioperative outcomes in patients with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome undergoing general anesthesia: a retrospective matched-pair study
papers.authors: Steinkirchner FM, Kaufmann CK, Kraus RF, Käss M, Schieffer E, Graf BM, Lassen C, Kimmerling V, Dejaco A
papers.summary: The study looked back at hospital records of 15 people with ME/CFS who had surgery under general anaesthesia and compared them with 15 similar patients without ME/CFS. Blood pressure and heart rate during surgery were equally well controlled in both groups. Afterwards, people with ME/CFS had clearly more pain and more often needed stronger painkillers.
papers.why: Practical safety information: general anaesthesia itself seems manageable in ME/CFS, but pain after surgery may need extra attention.

papers.title: Association between light exposure patterns and multidimensional health outcomes in individuals with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Cambras T, Domingo JC, Sanmartín-Sentañes R, Alegre-Martín J, Castro-Marrero J
papers.summary: 100 ME/CFS patients and 56 healthy people wore wrist sensors for light and activity for one week. The researchers found four patterns of daily light exposure. Patients with steady daylight had less fatigue and slept better than patients who got little light during the day.
papers.why: The amount of daylight goes along with how bad symptoms are. Light exposure is a cheap and simple thing that future treatment plans could test.

papers.title: iPSC-Derived Myogenic Progenitor Cells from People with ME/CFS Reveal Altered Genes and Pathways with Drug Repurposing Potential
papers.authors: Nguyen D, Truong TTT, Panizzutti B, Ellis M, Spolding B, Swinton C, Bortolasci CC, Bryce J, Smith J, Field C, Liu ZS, Kim JH, Berk M, Walder K
papers.summary: Researchers grew muscle precursor cells in the lab from stem cells of ME/CFS patients. These cells showed changed activity in genes for cell division, DNA repair, immune response and muscle structure. They also used some nutrients for energy differently from cells of healthy people.
papers.why: Lab evidence that ME/CFS muscle cells differ at the molecular level and are not just out of shape. A computer analysis named 22 existing drugs, including leflunomide, melatonin and midodrine, that could be tested. This is an early preprint based on a lab model and has not been peer-reviewed.

papers.title: Sex- and Menopause-Related Differences in Immune and Gastrointestinal Symptom Architecture in ME/CFS: Evidence from Factor Analysis and Structural Equation Modeling
papers.authors: Habermann-Horstmeier L, Horstmeier LM
papers.summary: In survey data from 748 ME/CFS patients in Germany, immune-type symptoms (such as sore throat or swollen glands) and gut symptoms grouped differently in women and men. In women they were more separate, in men more mixed. Menopause changed women's immune symptoms but not their gut symptoms.
papers.why: A follow-up on the same German patient group. ME/CFS may need subgroups by sex and menopause status, which matters for targeted drug trials.

papers.title: Efficacy and safety of rivaroxaban, colchicine, and famotidine-loratadine with specialist supportive clinical care for fatigue in patients with post-COVID-19 condition in the UK: a multisite, open-label, randomised controlled trial
papers.authors: Wall EC, Prescott G, Dehbi HM, Scott J, Evans RA, et al. (STIMULATE-ICP consortium)
papers.summary: 778 people in the UK with long-COVID fatigue got standard care alone or standard care plus one of three existing drugs for 12 weeks: an anti-inflammatory (colchicine), a blood thinner (rivaroxaban) or an antihistamine combination (famotidine-loratadine). Two of the drugs reduced fatigue a little more than standard care. The advantage was gone by week 24, after the drugs were stopped.
papers.why: Participants had general long-COVID fatigue, not a formal ME/CFS or PEM diagnosis. Still, it is one of the largest trials of repurposed drugs for this fatigue, and the benefit was small and short-lived. Treatments aimed at a specific mechanism are likely needed.

papers.title: Australian registry reports poor health and wellbeing in people living with ME/CFS
papers.authors: Eaton-Fitch N, Marshall-Gradisnik S
papers.summary: Using Australia's ME/CFS patient registry (2,873 patients and 797 healthy people), researchers found much worse quality of life in ME/CFS. Patients' symptoms fell into four distinct patterns.
papers.why: One of the largest registry studies on the burden of ME/CFS. It supports subgroups within the illness, which matters for targeted trials and for choosing a standard set of diagnostic criteria.

papers.title: Vagal cholinergic denervation of the gastric mucosa in Long-COVID-19: in vivo evidence of structural autonomic dysfunction
papers.authors: Acanfora D, Nolano M, Acanfora C, Colella C, Provitera V, Caporaso G, Rengo G, Antonelli Incalzi R, Casucci G
papers.summary: Small biopsies of the stomach lining from 12 long-COVID patients and 8 healthy people showed fewer fibres of the vagus nerve in the patients. The vagus nerve helps control digestion, heart rate and blood pressure.
papers.why: One of the first physical signs of vagus-nerve damage after a viral illness, relevant to problems with automatic body functions such as dizziness on standing. The study is very small and needs to be repeated.

papers.title: Implications of RNA virus persistence for post-acute sequelae and chronic inflammatory syndromes
papers.authors: Vidal D, de Araújo Castro Í, López CB
papers.summary: This review in a leading journal argues that RNA viruses such as SARS-CoV-2 can leave traces in the body, like viral genetic material or proteins, long after the infection is over. These remnants may keep inflammation going in long-lasting post-infection illnesses.
papers.why: Support from a top journal for the leftover-virus theory of ME/CFS and long COVID. It summarises existing evidence and contains no new experiments.

papers.title: Persistent impairments in muscle function and symptom burden in post-COVID syndrome: a prospective longitudinal study
papers.authors: Wunderle M, Ribeiro A, Lethen I, Schmaderer C, Wallraven T
papers.summary: 102 post-COVID patients and 102 recovered people were followed for six months. A simple grip-strength test, measuring force and how fast it fades, stayed abnormal in the patients the whole time. A weaker grip at the start predicted worse fatigue and lower mood six months later.
papers.why: Grip strength could serve as a simple, objective measure of muscle-related symptoms after COVID. This fits the muscle mechanism that Wirth and Scheibenbogen propose for ME/CFS, although the study is not from their group.

papers.title: Repeated Handgrip Strength Variability in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: Separating Disease-Related Fatigability from Force Gradation
papers.authors: Steinkirchner FM, Irrgang F, Kimmerling V, Kaess M, Popkirov S, Schieffer E, Gruber M, Dejaco A
papers.summary: ME/CFS patients squeezed a grip-strength device many times, and the researchers analysed how the strength changed from squeeze to squeeze. The aim was to separate normal tiring with effort from the disease-specific loss of energy in ME/CFS.
papers.why: A more precise measure of muscle fatigability could give drug trials a cheap, objective way to check whether a treatment helps, without relying only on patients' own reports.

papers.title: Low-Dose Ionizing Radiation and Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS): A Review
papers.authors: Rusin A, Cocchetto A, Mothersill C
papers.summary: This review puts forward an untested idea. Low-dose radiation, far below the level that causes radiation sickness, might trigger some of the same cell-damage signals seen in ME/CFS: tired mitochondria, a stress-protein pattern and an overactive immune system. The authors say clearly that no study has shown radiation causing ME/CFS in people.
papers.why: A new angle on possible triggers with markers that could be checked in future studies. It is speculative for now.

papers.title: Risks of autoimmune and inflammatory post-acute COVID-19 conditions: a network cohort study
papers.authors: Burkard TM, et al.
papers.summary: This large study compared people who tested positive for COVID-19 with similar people who tested negative and tracked whether the positive group later developed more autoimmune and inflammatory conditions, including ME/CFS. In the first nine months after infection, ME/CFS diagnoses were not more common in the COVID-positive group.
papers.why: This argues against a large short-term rise in ME/CFS diagnoses after COVID-19. Other studies do find one, and ME/CFS is often diagnosed only well after nine months, so the result may reflect slow diagnosis rather than no risk.

papers.title: Pacing and energy management with digital tools for conditions with chronic fatigue: What we know so far in ME/CFS and Long COVID
papers.authors: Sanal-Hayes NEM, Hayes LD, Mclaughlin M, Sculthorpe NF
papers.summary: This article reviews wearables and smartphone apps meant to help people with ME/CFS and long COVID pace themselves, that is, stay within a safe activity limit to avoid a crash. The authors' own 6-month trial of an activity tracker with alerts (PaceMe) was safe and helped people feel more in control. It did not reduce crashes more than standard care.
papers.why: Digital pacing tools can help with self-awareness and safety. So far they have not been shown to prevent crashes, so expectations should stay modest.

papers.title: Wearable Heart Rate Variability Monitoring, Autonomic Dysfunction and Post-exertional Malaise in Long COVID: An Observational Study
papers.authors: Ruijgt TM, Slaghekke A, Ellens A, Janssen KW, Wüst RCI
papers.summary: 121 people with long COVID and 21 healthy people wore heart-rate monitors for several days. Patients had lower heart-rate variability, a measure of the body's rest-and-recover nervous system, around exercise and during sleep. This signal stayed abnormal for a full 24 hours after exertion, especially once activity passed a certain intensity.
papers.why: A wearable can show a concrete limit for how much exertion leads to a crash. That could help with pacing and give drug trials an objective outcome.

papers.title: High Quality Analysis of Circulating Biomarkers Reveals No Evidence of Elevated Inflammatory Markers in a Long COVID Cohort Recruited at a Primary Care Center
papers.authors: Torres ML, Lerma-Irureta D, Ibañez-Ruiz J, Lucas A, Magallón-Botaya R, Schoorlemmer J
papers.summary: Using a more precise blood test than earlier studies, researchers measured common inflammation markers (CRP, TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6) in long-COVID patients from a Spanish GP practice. The markers were not higher than in recovered or healthy people.
papers.why: Simple inflammation markers in the blood do not reliably diagnose or explain long COVID. The cause probably lies elsewhere, for example in microclots or faulty immune cells.

papers.title: An Open-Label Feasibility Study of Remdesivir in Long COVID: Results from the ERASE LC Trial
papers.authors: Faghy MA, Chynoweth J, Barnett A, Skipper L, Allgar V, Neilens H, Sands K, Lord A, Hambly H, Aspinall P, Rollinson C, Strain W, Owen R, Thomas C, Grigg M, Kranen S, Mokbel K, Razak H, Ashton R, Maidment I, Bewick T
papers.summary: 73 people with long COVID in the UK got a 5-day infusion of the antiviral drug remdesivir. The study checked whether this was feasible and safe, not yet whether it works. Almost everyone finished the treatment safely, and patients reported somewhat less fatigue and better walking. The authors say a randomised trial with a comparison group is needed to know whether the drug caused this.
papers.why: The first test of an antiviral, rather than an immune-calming drug, for long COVID. Targeting leftover virus long after the infection is still an open question, also for ME/CFS-like illness.

papers.title: ME/CFS and the thalamus as a precision gate: what reversible thalamocortical connectivity reveals about central gain in post-infectious fatigue
papers.authors: Strube A
papers.summary: This is an opinion piece, not a new study. It builds on a recent Charité study showing that the thalamus, a relay station deep in the brain that filters sensory and body signals, works differently in ME/CFS and moved partly back towards normal after hyperbaric oxygen therapy. The author suggests that many ME/CFS symptoms that seem unrelated, such as sensitivity to light, sound and touch, pain, dizziness on standing and brain fog, could all come from this filter being turned up too high.
papers.why: One brain-based explanation for very different symptoms, which could lead to treatments aimed at one control point. It rests on a single earlier study and still needs to be tested.

papers.title: Altered TRPM3-Dependent Cytosolic and Mitochondrial Calcium Influx in Natural Killer Cells of Post-COVID-19 Condition Patients
papers.authors: Magawa CT, Eaton-Fitch N, Muraki K, Marshall-Gradisnik S, et al.
papers.summary: Researchers looked at natural killer (NK) cells, a type of immune cell, in 8 people with lasting post-COVID illness and 8 healthy people. In the patients' cells a calcium channel called TRPM3 was faulty. Too little calcium entered the cell, too much built up in the mitochondria, and the cells barely reacted when stimulated.
papers.why: The same faulty channel was first found in ME/CFS immune cells. Finding it after COVID suggests that both illnesses share an immune and energy problem, which could be a common treatment target.

papers.title: Wearable-derived cardiopulmonary fitness and physical activity in adults with long COVID: a RECOVER-Adult digital health substudy
papers.authors: Vogel JM, Jenkins T, Cerda M, Chen H, Goldman J, Katz SD, et al., RECOVER Consortium
papers.summary: Almost 1,500 people wore fitness trackers about 21 months after COVID-19. Those with many long-COVID symptoms had lower heart-rate variability at rest, a faster resting pulse and were much less active day to day than those with few symptoms.
papers.why: Wearable data, not just questionnaires, show a lasting drop in heart and activity fitness almost two years after infection. Whether long COVID becomes a long-term risk for heart health is an open question.

papers.title: Effect of low-dose naltrexone for long COVID: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Byambasuren O, Atkins T, Baptista S, Glasziou P, Chakraborty S
papers.summary: This review pooled the available studies on low-dose naltrexone (LDN), a cheap generic drug that many people with long COVID and ME/CFS use off-label, to see whether it helps with symptoms such as fatigue.
papers.why: LDN is one of the treatments patients try most often. An independent review of the evidence helps decide whether it deserves a proper clinical trial.

papers.title: Low serum selenium combined with SELENOP-autoantibodies are associated with persistent fatigue after SARS-CoV-2 infection
papers.authors: Schmidt B, Asaad S, Mavarani L, Stang A, Chillon TS, Minich WB, Renko K, Brenner T, Schöler LM, Dittmer U, Trilling M, Schomburg L
papers.summary: Selenium is a mineral the body needs, and SELENOP is the blood protein that carries it. In about 750 adults roughly two years after COVID-19, people with low selenium and antibodies against SELENOP were more likely to still have fatigue. A selenium shortage, possibly made worse by the immune system attacking its carrier, may add to lasting tiredness.
papers.why: Selenium plus SELENOP antibodies is an easy-to-measure marker for post-viral fatigue. Whether selenium supplements help could be tested in a trial.

papers.title: Molecular, cellular and network mapping of brain structural deviations in patients with Post-COVID19 syndrome
papers.authors: Martins D, Cai Z, Mariani N, Borsini A, Mondelli V, Eiff B, Rota S, van Wamelen D, Nicholson T, Rida L, Hampshire A, Fernandes L, Zelaya F, Podlewska A, Chaudhuri R, Turkheimer F, Williams SCR, Veronese M
