papers.summary: Brain scans of 20 people with lasting tiredness after a mild COVID-19 infection showed small changes in thickness in certain brain regions. These were mainly regions rich in the protein the coronavirus uses to enter cells, and regions involved in mood and the messenger serotonin.
papers.why: Brain scans show that fatigue can follow even a mild infection and link it to specific biology, such as virus entry points and serotonin circuits, that could become drug targets.

papers.title: Increased Mannosylation of Extracellular Vesicles in Long COVID Plasma as a Binding Target for Galanthus nivalis Agglutinin (GNA) Affinity Resin
papers.authors: Pesqueira Sanchez MA, de Necochea Campion R, Dalhuisen T, Fehrman EA, Chhabra PS, Kelly JD, Martin JN, Deeks SG, Henrich TJ, Peluso MJ, LaRosa SP
papers.summary: Cells release tiny particles into the blood called extracellular vesicles (EVs). In people with long COVID these particles carry unusual sugar coatings. The researchers showed that a sugar-binding material from a plant can pull these coated particles out of blood. That could lead to a diagnostic test and to a way of filtering them from the blood.
papers.why: From the well-known LIINC long-COVID group at UCSF. A new biomarker idea and a possible blood-filtering treatment, similar in principle to immunoadsorption.

papers.title: Exploring differences in protein cargo of extracellular vesicles from ME/CFS patient plasma compared to healthy controls
papers.authors: Rydland A, Yran ES, Nyman TA, Strand EB, Trøseid AS, Øvstebø R, Heinicke F, Lie BA, Viken MK
papers.summary: The study looked at tiny particles that cells release into the blood (extracellular vesicles) in 49 ME/CFS patients and 50 healthy people. Patients had more of these particles, and some of the proteins they carried differed. None of these protein differences held up after strict statistical correction.
papers.why: The largest study of these particles in ME/CFS so far. The result is exploratory, but it adds a Norwegian patient group to a line of biomarker research that also includes work from Scheibenbogen's group.

papers.title: A comparative analysis of computational clustering methods for symptom-based classification of long COVID
papers.authors: Green TD, McWilliams C, de Figueiredo L, Soares L, Pollack B, Cohen AK, Zhi-Xuan T, Falor T, Davis HE
papers.summary: Patient researchers analysed answers from more than 6,000 people with long COVID about 162 symptoms and used three different computer methods to sort them into subtypes. The methods mostly disagreed about which subtypes exist, so long-COVID symptoms look more like a spectrum than clear categories. People with more symptoms overall always had worse post-exertional malaise and were more often women.
papers.why: A warning for research on subtypes in long COVID and ME/CFS: which subtype a patient lands in may depend on the statistical method more than on real biology. Trials that select subgroups need to keep this in mind.

papers.title: Chronic Fatigue Syndrome in Long COVID: prevalence and impact on health-related quality of life and health status. A cross-sectional study. BioICOPER study
papers.authors: Navarro-Cáceres A, Gómez-Sánchez L, Suárez-Moreno N, Arroyo-Romero S, Domínguez-Martín A, Lugones-Sánchez C, González-Sánchez S, Castro-Rivero AB, Gómez-Marcos MA, Navarro-Matías EN
papers.summary: Among 304 people with long COVID in Spain, a sizeable group met older formal criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome. This group had clearly worse quality of life and general health than the other long-COVID patients.
papers.why: It shows how large and how badly affected the ME/CFS-like group within long COVID is, which matters for how these patients are defined, studied and prioritised.

papers.title: Pilot longitudinal integrated transcriptomic-metabolomic study reveals immune and metabolic signatures in non-hospitalized healthcare workers with long COVID
papers.authors: Espín E, Yang C, Shannon CP, Checkervarty AK, Kim S, Lapp L, Assadian S, Grunau B, Goldfarb DM, Hutton J, Huan T, Tebbutt SJ
papers.journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
papers.summary: Healthcare workers who developed long COVID after a mild infection, with fatigue and brain fog as main symptoms, had unusual patterns in their immune-cell genes and blood chemistry compared with colleagues who fully recovered.
papers.why: Most biomarker studies look at people who were in hospital. This one looks at the milder, more ME/CFS-like form that is harder to study but affects many more people.

papers.title: Components and Delivery Formats of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Chronic Fatigue Syndrome/Myalgic Encephalomyelitis: A Systematic Review and Component Network Meta-Analysis
papers.authors: Wang S, Ren J, Fang S, Hao Q, Zhang YQ, Kong L, Fang M
papers.summary: This analysis of 16 trials looked at cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), a talking therapy, in ME/CFS. Guided self-help and one-to-one CBT reduced fatigue right after treatment. Goal-setting and acceptance-based techniques helped. Teaching patients facts about the illness on its own may not have helped.
papers.why: CBT is controversial in ME/CFS. This study looks at which parts of it help and which do not, which is useful for designing psychological support that runs alongside medical treatment.

papers.title: Efficacy of acupuncture-based traditional Chinese medicine therapies for chronic fatigue syndrome: systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Li Y, Liang G, Xiao T, Xu L
papers.summary: Pooling 8 trials with 715 patients, acupuncture reduced overall, physical and mental fatigue more than the comparison treatments, with no difference in side effects. The authors say the trials were small and of mixed quality.
papers.why: Acupuncture has some trial evidence against fatigue in ME/CFS, but the evidence is weak, as the authors themselves point out.

papers.title: The physio-affective symptoms of Long COVID are strongly predicted by the severity of the acute infectious phase, and lowered antioxidants, nitric oxide, and alanine transaminase levels
papers.authors: Maes M, Tunvirachaisakul C, Semeão LdO, Michelin AP, Matsumoto AK, Brinholi FF, Barbosa DS, Zhang Y, Sodsai P, Hirankarn N, Almulla AF
papers.summary: 71 long-COVID patients were followed for six months. Mood symptoms, ME/CFS-type fatigue, breathing problems and nerve symptoms rose and fell together as one package. How severe the original COVID infection was, including low levels of antioxidants and nitric oxide, strongly predicted how bad this package became.
papers.why: Measurements taken during the first infection might show who is heading for the more severe, ME/CFS-like form of long COVID, so these patients could be watched closely or treated early.

papers.title: Disrupted glymphatic function and its relationship with sleep and cognitive impairment in ME/CFS assessed via DTI-ALPS
papers.authors: Thapaliya K, Marshall-Gradisnik S, Inderyas M, Barnden L
papers.summary: A scan method that measures how well the brain clears waste during sleep was used in 31 people with ME/CFS and 27 healthy people. The patients' brain clearance was clearly weaker, especially on the right side. People with worse sleep and worse concentration and memory had the weakest clearance.
papers.why: Slow waste removal in the brain during sleep could help explain brain fog and poor sleep in ME/CFS. It also gives researchers something new to measure.

papers.title: Immunoadsorption Versus Sham Treatment for Post-COVID Syndrome: A Randomised Sham-Controlled Crossover Trial
papers.authors: Stortz M, Kommer A, Meineck M, Boedecker-Lips SC, Claßen P, Tomalla V, Rausch F, Lang LS, Wild PS, Schmidtmann I, Weinmann A, Kraus D, Weinmann-Menke J
papers.summary: In this trial in Mainz, Germany, 40 people with lasting post-COVID symptoms and high levels of self-attacking antibodies had these antibodies filtered out of their blood (immunoadsorption) or got a sham version of the same procedure. The real treatment removed the antibodies, but patients did not feel better than after the sham, and side effects were more common.
papers.why: A careful, placebo-controlled trial with a negative result for removing these antibodies, an approach other German studies, including Scheibenbogen's, are also testing. Taking the antibodies out did not by itself relieve symptoms, at least in this set-up.

papers.title: Global and local genetic overlap among ME/CFS, irritable bowel syndrome and psychiatric traits: a hypothesis-generating analysis
papers.authors: Lee JH
papers.summary: This study compared the genetics of ME/CFS with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), depression and loneliness using large databases. Overall, ME/CFS shared a lot of genetic background with IBS and depression. At the level of specific places in the genome, very little of this overlap held up. Genes linked to ME/CFS were concentrated in nerve cells, including those in the gut, and not in brain circuits linked to depression.
papers.why: ME/CFS, IBS and depression often occur together, but ME/CFS seems to have its own genetic roots in the nervous system. It is not a form of depression and needs medical research of its own.

papers.title: Higher-order brain processes, rather than early processing, underlie sensory problems in ME/CFS: evidence from ERPs
papers.authors: Kumar S, Veldhuis A, Yazdani F
papers.summary: Brain-wave recordings (ERPs) during sound tests in 31 people with ME/CFS and 30 healthy people showed normal basic sound processing. A later brain signal linked to attention and mental effort was weaker in ME/CFS.
papers.why: Sensory overload in ME/CFS seems to come from how the brain handles attention and higher processing, not from the senses themselves. Treatments would need to target that higher level.

papers.title: Development and initial content validation of the Vienna Post-Exertional Malaise Questionnaire: an iterative mixed-methods study
papers.authors: Pimminger T, Ahrens-Schwabe A, Fragner T, Brandl T, Kotzian S, Wüst RC, Waldhör T, Kapan A
papers.summary: A team in Austria worked with patients and experts over several rounds to build a new 13-question survey that measures post-exertional malaise (PEM), the crash after activity that is the main symptom of ME/CFS.
papers.why: A questionnaire built with patients and made just for PEM could improve diagnosis and become a standard outcome in drug trials. Full validation is still to come.

papers.title: Therapeutic plasma exchange and immunomodulatory strategies in post-infectious syndromes: A review of immune dysregulation in PTLDS, long COVID, ME/CFS, and PANS/PANDAS
papers.authors: Kaplan G
papers.summary: This review argues that ME/CFS, long COVID, chronic Lyme disease and some post-infectious conditions in children all involve a similar immune misfire, with inflammation and self-attacking antibodies. It discusses whether blood-filtering treatments such as plasma exchange could help.
papers.why: The author thinks earlier large trials of these treatments failed partly because they did not use biomarkers to choose patients likely to benefit. Future ME/CFS trials could learn from that.

papers.title: Mapping the Symptom Profile and Burden of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS): Insights from the TIMES Survey
papers.authors: Tyson SF, Fleming R
papers.summary: More than 1,000 adults with ME/CFS filled in a detailed symptom questionnaire. On average their symptom burden was severe. Cognitive problems such as brain fog were rated worst, fatigue was the most common symptom, and women reported more symptoms than men.
papers.why: One of the largest patient surveys on symptom burden in ME/CFS. It describes rather than explains, but it shows how disabling the illness is and helps choose outcomes for drug trials.

papers.title: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy improves clinical symptoms and functional capacity and modulates thalamic connectivity in ME/CFS: a prospective cohort study
papers.authors: Kim L, Cammà G, Peters CK, Mantwill M, Müller O, Leprêtre N, Heindrich C, Rust R, Krill M, Hartung TJ, Reeß LG, Krohn S, Heymann CV, Wittke K, Finke C, Scheibenbogen C
papers.summary: ME/CFS patients who had hyperbaric oxygen treatment, breathing pure oxygen in a pressurised chamber, had fewer symptoms and better physical function. Brain scans also showed changes in an area linked to fatigue.
papers.why: Carmen Scheibenbogen's team was involved. It is one of the first studies to link improvement after oxygen treatment with measurable brain changes. There was no placebo group.

papers.title: Low Vasopressin in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Huhmar HM, Soinne LS, Bertilson BC, Ghatan PH, Bragée BA, Polo OJ
papers.summary: Levels of vasopressin, a hormone that helps control water balance, blood flow and stress responses, were lower in ME/CFS patients than in healthy people.
papers.why: Low vasopressin could explain dizziness, strong thirst and fatigue. It might become a diagnostic marker or a treatment target.

papers.title: Dynamic microclot profiling: thromboelastography advances precision management in long COVID and myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Saleem S, Hussain A, Haroon M, Raza A, Afzal U, Anwar MF, Imran S, Iqbal MU, Hajj F
papers.summary: A special clotting test was used to measure tiny blood clots (microclots) in people with long COVID and ME/CFS. Clotting patterns differed from person to person, which could guide individual treatment.
papers.why: More evidence that abnormal clotting and poor circulation play a role. The method could help find patients who might benefit from anti-clotting treatment.

papers.title: Elevated serum levels of interleukin-11 and matrix metalloproteinase-9 in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Chinnappan B, Kempuraj D, Aenlle KK, Middleton A, Day KS, Kothuru SP, Joshi RS, Klimas NG, Theoharides TC
papers.summary: Two inflammation-related substances were raised in patients' blood. They were linked to immune cells that react to Epstein-Barr virus, the cause of glandular fever.
papers.why: The two substances could serve as a blood marker, and the link to a common virus suggests new treatment ideas.

papers.title: Tryptophan Metabolism and Aryl-Hydrocarbon Receptor Agonists in the Gut Microbiome of People With Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Esteban DJ, Conrad B, Cullinan A, et al.
papers.summary: Gut bacteria of ME/CFS patients process the nutrient tryptophan differently and make fewer of the molecules that help keep the immune system calm.
papers.why: The gut could be a way to influence the immune system, which supports treatment ideas based on gut bacteria and immunity.

papers.title: Systems neuroendocrinology in ME/CFS and long COVID: a chronobiological framework for hormone-based research
papers.authors: Thomas N, Huang K, Schneider-Futschik EK, et al.
papers.summary: The authors argue that hormone studies in ME/CFS and long COVID contradict each other because they ignore the time of day and the phase of the menstrual cycle. They recommend taking both into account.
papers.why: Better hormone studies could reveal treatment targets. The paper gives practical advice for trials, especially those with mostly female participants.

papers.title: Gastrointestinal symptoms correlate with core clinical features and systemic inflammation in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Brown M, Vernon SD, Indart AC, Green PH, Alaedini A
papers.summary: The worse a patient's gut symptoms, the worse their main ME/CFS symptoms and the inflammation in the body tended to be. The gut seems to be part of the illness.
papers.why: Gut problems should be taken seriously in ME/CFS care. This could change who is included in drug trials and how improvement is measured.

papers.title: Long-Term Follow-Up of Women with Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS): A 16-Year Longitudinal Study
papers.authors: Tomić S, Pastornački A, Drljača M, Glogovac J, Bošković V, Brkić S
papers.summary: 20 women with ME/CFS were followed for 16 years. 85% developed other serious illnesses, including rheumatoid arthritis, cancer, depression and heart disease.
papers.why: One of the longest follow-ups in ME/CFS. The many added illnesses show how urgently treatment is needed, and the pattern may point to shared biological causes.

papers.title: Two-timepoint multidomain follow-up of post-COVID condition and ME/CFS: overlapping autonomic, small-fiber, and cognitive changes
papers.authors: Azcue N, Barranco C, Tijero-Merino B, Acera M, Fernández-Valle T, Lafuente JV, Gabilondo I, Ruiz-Lopez M, Del Pino R, Gómez-Esteban JC
papers.summary: Post-COVID and ME/CFS patients were followed for almost three years. Their changes in nerves, blood-pressure control and thinking speed were largely the same, and post-COVID patients looked more and more like established ME/CFS over time.
papers.why: Evidence over time that post-COVID and ME/CFS share the same disease process. Treatments that work for one may work for both.

papers.title: Cluster analysis of ME/CFS symptoms in DecodeME reveals two subgroups and a link to onset type
papers.authors: St-Jean C, Dibble JJ, Ponting CP, Prigge R
papers.summary: Using symptom surveys from more than 19,000 people with ME/CFS in the UK DecodeME study, researchers found two broad groups. Just over half had a heavy symptom load in almost every body system. The rest had milder symptoms. People who fell ill after an infection, rather than gradually, and women were more often in the heavier group.
papers.why: ME/CFS is not one uniform illness. At least two patterns exist, linked to how the illness began. That can help trials choose more similar patient groups. No single gene explained the split.

papers.title: Symptomatic hypermobility as a risk factor for Long COVID with high post-exertional symptom exacerbation: further analysis of data from a retrospective online survey of adults in the United States and United Kingdom
papers.authors: Lubell J, Torok RA, Rudy RM, Quadt L, Eccles JA
papers.summary: In a survey of more than 1,800 adults who had COVID-19, people with symptomatic hypermobility (unusually loose joints that cause problems) who also had dizziness on standing or brain fog were about 9 to 10 times more likely to develop severe long COVID with strong crashes after physical or mental activity.
papers.why: Independent support for a link between loose connective tissue and crashes after exertion, the same link Klaus Wirth proposed in his May 2026 paper. The authors are not connected to Wirth.

papers.title: Metabolomic Classification of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome via Explainable Ensemble Learning and Pareto-Guided Feature Selection
papers.authors: Yagin FH, Korkmaz Y, Colak C, Alzakari SA, Alkhalifa AK, Al-Hashem F, Aghaei M
papers.summary: Using blood metabolite profiles from 197 people (106 with ME/CFS, 91 healthy), a machine-learning model told patients from healthy people with high accuracy. The strongest clues were a changed tryptophan pathway, which the body uses to make mood-related messengers, and signs of poor energy production in the mitochondria.
papers.why: Another step towards a blood test for ME/CFS. It points again to failing mitochondrial energy and a disturbed tryptophan pathway.

papers.title: Biomarkers of post-acute infection syndrome: a systematic literature review
papers.authors: Wendt K, Schieck M, Gille C, Marschollek M, Illig T, Wolff D, Nee S
papers.summary: This review of 142 studies on ME/CFS and long COVID found that a signalling pathway called NF-κB, a switch that turns on inflammation, keeps showing up across many lab findings. There were also shared changes in amino acid, energy, fat and gut-bacteria metabolism.
papers.why: From Hannover Medical School, Germany. It puts the scattered biomarker research into one framework, which helps future work on diagnostic tests and drug targets.

papers.title: Exploratory Dried Blood Spot Metabolomics Identifies Pathway-Level Convergence with ME/CFS Biology in a Self-Reported PEM-like Fatigue Phenotype
papers.authors: Hauguel P, Anctil N, Noel L
papers.summary: Finger-prick blood spots from 1,784 people in a large community health study were tested for metabolic substances. People who reported crashes after activity showed the same kind of changes in energy production, fats and stress hormones that earlier studies found in diagnosed ME/CFS. The method is cheaper and works for many more people than earlier blood studies.
papers.why: ME/CFS-like metabolic changes might be detectable in the general population with a cheap finger-prick test. That could be a way to screen on a large scale.

papers.title: Rationale and Design of RECOVER-ENERGIZE: A Platform Clinical Trial of Interventions for Exercise Intolerance With and Without Post-exertional Malaise in Long COVID
papers.authors: Friedly J, Bateman L, Berdan LG, Casaburi R, Erdmann N, Felker GM, Itchon-Ramos N, Keteyian SJ, MacIntyre N, O'Brien L, Reist C, Rossiter HB, Silverstein A, Taylor E, Pike Welch H, Yanez ND, Zimmerman KO, Make B
papers.summary: This paper describes the design of a large US trial, with no results yet. It is a platform trial, a flexible set-up that can test several treatments over time under one shared structure, for exercise intolerance and post-exertional malaise in long COVID. It runs within the NIH's RECOVER initiative.
papers.why: A large NIH-funded trial set up specifically for PEM and exercise intolerance, where good trials are still rare. Known ME/CFS exercise researchers such as Lucinda Bateman and Harry Rossiter are involved. First results are still to come.

papers.title: Central noradrenergic deficiency in post-infectious chronic fatigue: neurobehavioral correlates
papers.authors: Aregawi L, Walitt B, Sullivan P, Norato G, Benjamin RN, Goldstein DS
papers.summary: Researchers at the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) tested spinal fluid from 16 people with ME/CFS, 34 with long COVID, 32 with Parkinson's disease and 40 healthy volunteers. They measured two brain messengers: noradrenaline, which drives alertness and the fight-or-flight response, and dopamine. People with ME/CFS had clearly less noradrenaline activity than healthy people, even less than the long-COVID and Parkinson's groups. Dopamine was normal. Lower noradrenaline went with weaker grip endurance and worse general health, and it was lowest in people with post-exertional malaise (PEM).
papers.why: The study links a measurable shortage in the brain to muscle fatigue and symptom severity. The authors think making noradrenaline may cost more energy than ME/CFS cells can supply. Boosting noradrenaline signalling could be a drug target.

papers.title: Biological Insights from Genome-Wide Association Studies and Whole Genome Sequencing of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Maccallini P
papers.summary: This analysis combined two large genetic studies, the UK's DecodeME and the US Million Veteran Program, with almost 20,000 patients and 700,000 people without ME/CFS. The strongest repeated signals were in brain genes, especially genes at glutamatergic synapses (the junctions where nerve cells use the messenger glutamate). Genes active in the blood did not stand out.
papers.why: Two of the biggest genetic datasets point to the same brain genes. That supports a brain-based biological process in ME/CFS and names pathways that future drugs could target.

papers.title: Involvement of autoantibodies against G protein-coupled receptors in post-COVID condition and Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Azcue N, Prada A, Del Pino R, Acera M, Fernández-Valle T, Ayo-Mentxakatorre N, Pérez-Concha T, Murueta-Goyena A, Lafuente JV, López de Munain A, Ruiz Irastorza G, Ribacoba L, Gabilondo I, Tijero-Merino B, Gómez-Esteban JC
papers.summary: Researchers measured autoantibodies against the body's own receptors for stress hormones and nerve signals in 96 people with post-COVID condition, 59 with ME/CFS and 36 healthy people. People with ME/CFS had more of one of these antibodies, against the beta-2-adrenergic receptor. Higher levels went with worse control of blood pressure and heart rate and with slower thinking.
papers.why: Another result that fits the idea that these antibodies drive ME/CFS symptoms. The same idea is behind Scheibenbogen's immunoadsorption studies (IMPACT, IA-Surv). This study comes from a separate group in the Basque Country, Spain.

papers.title: Risk factors for severe post-COVID condition in children, adolescents, and young adults
papers.authors: Donath Q, Haegele M, Schindler D, Welzhofer T, Christa C, Grabbe A, Leone A, Ilhan C, Weidmann C, Eberhartinger M, Bechtold S, Bursch N, Wolf H, Hieber H, Peo LC, Bucka LA, Stojanov S, Warlitz C, Alberer M, Gerrer K, Hausruckinger A, Mittelstrass K, Wendtner CM, Hoechstetter MA, Grübl A, Toepfner N, Pricoco R, Scheibenbogen C, Mihatsch LL, Behrends U
papers.summary: A German study looked at 120 young people aged 7 to 25 with lasting COVID symptoms. Having 12 or more symptoms during the infection, plus dizziness or near-fainting (a sign that blood flow is poorly regulated when standing), strongly predicted the most severe form of the illness. 24% of this group were later diagnosed with ME/CFS.
papers.why: Doctors get an early warning list for children at risk of a severe course with ME/CFS after COVID. Scheibenbogen is a co-author.

papers.title: Human Endogenous Retroviruses in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: Emerging Roles in Pathogenesis, Immunity, Biomarkers and Therapeutics
papers.authors: Perera KD, Oltra E, Carding SR
papers.summary: This review explains that our DNA contains old virus fragments called human endogenous retroviruses (HERVs). They are normally silent. Common infections such as Epstein-Barr virus, HHV-6 or COVID-19 may switch some of them back on, and this could feed the immune problems and brain inflammation seen in ME/CFS.
papers.why: It offers a concrete explanation for why an infection can lead to long-term illness. Measuring which HERVs are active could become a diagnostic test or a way to follow treatment.

papers.title: Comprehensive Immunophenotyping of Monocytes and Dendritic Cells Suggests Distinct Pathophysiology in Chronic Fatigue Syndrome and Long COVID
papers.authors: Petrov S, Bozhkova M, Ivanovska M, Kalfova T, Dudova D, Todorova Y, Dimitrova R, Murdjeva M, Taskov H, Nikolova M, Maes M
papers.summary: Detailed tests of immune cells in blood from 103 ME/CFS patients, 63 long-COVID patients and 41 healthy people showed that the two illnesses differ. In long COVID the immune system was still fighting but wearing out. In ME/CFS it was more suppressed and less coordinated.
papers.why: ME/CFS and long COVID can feel similar to patients, but their immune problems seem to differ. A treatment that works for one may not work for the other, which matters for trial design.

papers.title: Laxity Comes with Consequences: Connective Tissue Disorders and Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS)
papers.authors: Wirth KJ
papers.summary: Klaus Wirth suggests that loose, stretchy connective tissue, as in some joint-hypermobility conditions, and ME/CFS can make each other worse. Low oxygen and overactive immune cells in ME/CFS may weaken the links that hold collagen fibres together. In turn, loose ligaments and an unstable neck may trigger the blood-flow and blood-pressure problems of ME/CFS.
papers.why: From Wirth (Mitodicure). It extends his muscle and blood-flow theory to connective tissue and hypermobility, a link some patients report. It is an early preprint that has not been peer-reviewed, and other researchers have publicly questioned parts of it, so it is a working idea.

papers.title: Toward a Molecular Reclassification of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: Integrating Multi-Omics, Machine Learning, and Precision Medicine
papers.authors: Frank J, Nesterovitch N, Movva C, Klimas NG, Nathanson L
papers.summary: This review describes how methods that read thousands of gene and protein signals at once, together with artificial intelligence, are used to sort ME/CFS patients into biological groups based on what goes wrong in their bodies, not on symptoms alone.
papers.why: From Nancy Klimas's group in the US. It outlines how precision medicine could work in ME/CFS and names overactive innate immunity, exhausted T cells and failing cellular energy as the most likely first treatment targets.

papers.title: Comparative Gut Microbiome Alterations in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome and Long COVID-19 Syndrome
papers.authors: Donchev D, Nikolova R, Vaseva K, Taskov H, Murdjeva M, Maes M, Ivanov IN
papers.summary: The study compared gut bacteria in people with ME/CFS and people with long COVID. Both groups showed the same changes, mainly missing helpful bacteria and too many of others. Healthy people did not show these changes.
papers.why: The first direct comparison of gut bacteria in the two illnesses. The overlap suggests shared gut biology and possibly shared treatments, such as restoring the gut flora.

papers.title: Expert perspectives on myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome — Insights from the 3rd International Conference of the Charité Fatigue Center
papers.authors: Fehrer A, et al.
papers.summary: A summary of what experts agreed on at Charité's international ME/CFS conference: problems with circulation, the immune system and the body's energy use. It warns that steady research funding is urgently needed.
papers.why: It sets out the current priorities of Scheibenbogen's group and the reasoning behind their trials, including immunoadsorption and the planned inebilizumab study.

papers.title: A causal link between autoantibodies and neurological symptoms in long COVID
papers.authors: Santos Guedes de Sá K, Silva J, Bayarri-Olmos R, et al. (Iwasaki A, senior author)
papers.summary: Antibodies made during a COVID infection stay in people with long COVID. When transferred into mice, they caused fatigue, coordination problems and nerve damage. So these self-attacking antibodies can directly cause neurological symptoms.
papers.why: Published in Cell, one of the top science journals. It shows that autoantibodies can cause post-viral illness and supports the antibody-removing treatments being developed for ME/CFS.

papers.title: Irisin Signaling Resistance in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis: A Proposed Mechanistic Framework for Post-Exertional Malaise Involving the TSP-1-HSP90α-αvβ5 Axis
papers.authors: Souma B, Elremaly W, Akoume MY, Elbakry M, Godbout C, Moreau A
papers.summary: People with ME had lower levels of irisin, a hormone normally released during exercise, and reacted abnormally to it. Another protein, thrombospondin-1, was blocking it. This could explain why any exertion triggers a crash.
papers.why: It describes a new pathway behind post-exertional malaise and names thrombospondin-1 and its partners as possible drug targets.

papers.title: Raman Spectroscopy Combined with Machine Learning Reveals Myalgic Encephalomyelitis-Associated Biomolecular Signatures at Rest and After Standardized Stress
papers.authors: Heidarifard M, Moezzi A, Dallaire F, Ember K, Elremaly W, Caraus I, Franco A, Leblond F, Moreau A, Dehaes M
papers.summary: A light-based test (Raman spectroscopy) combined with AI told people with ME from healthy people correctly in about 80 to 85% of cases. It used chemical changes in blood plasma, at rest and after a standard stress test.
papers.why: A fast and possibly cheap screening test for an illness that has no objective test. It also works after exertion, when symptoms usually get worse.

papers.title: Reframing ME/CFS: toward a unified mechanistic model of chronic post-infectious diseases
papers.authors: Watton P, Prusty BK
papers.summary: A detailed review of how ME/CFS research moved from uncertainty to a clearer biological picture. Long-COVID research revealed several faults that act together: immune disruption, failing cellular power plants, damaged blood vessels and abnormal clotting. They often only show up when the body is under physical strain.
papers.why: From Bhupesh Prusty, whose lab showed that patients' antibodies can damage cellular energy machinery. The authors argue that trials should test patients under strain and choose them by these findings, which could make treatment more targeted.

papers.title: Investigation of BOLD signal intensities in long COVID patients using 7T functional MRI
papers.authors: Inderyas M, Thapaliya K, Marshall-Gradisnik S, Barnden L
papers.summary: Using a very strong 7-tesla MRI scanner, researchers compared brain activity in 19 people with long COVID and 27 healthy people during a thinking task. The patients had weaker activity in regions for attention and error checking, and this went with slower thinking and more pain.
papers.why: Detailed scans show that brain fog and fatigue in long COVID come with real changes in brain activity. The group also studies ME/CFS, which supports a shared biological basis.

papers.title: Brain dynamics of attentional, default-mode and limbic networks are disrupted at rest in post-COVID-19 syndrome
papers.authors: Cahart MS, O'Daly O, Cai Z, Mariani N, Borsini A, Mondelli V, Eiff B, Rota S, Nicholson T, Rida L, Hampshire A, Dipasquale O, Fernandes L, Turkheimer F, Williams SCR, Martins D
papers.summary: Brain scans at rest in 20 people with post-COVID syndrome and 20 healthy people showed that the patients' brains spent less time in an alert, outward-focused state and more time in an inward-focused, emotional state.
papers.why: Fatigue and brain fog after COVID may involve the brain getting stuck in a less outward-focused mode. This could one day become an objective test or a way to check treatments.

papers.title: Regulatory Cycles of Orexin and Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 in Postviral Syndromes
papers.authors: Ruhrländer J, Schieffer E, Schieffer B
papers.summary: Orexin is a brain messenger that keeps us awake and helps regulate energy use, sleep and hormones. This review argues that faulty orexin signalling, together with changes in the gut-brain hormone GLP-1, may help explain the exhaustion, sleep problems and metabolic changes in long COVID and ME/CFS.
papers.why: Both hormone systems already have approved drugs: orexin-targeting medicines and GLP-1 drugs used for diabetes and weight loss. They could be starting points for treating the underlying biology of ME/CFS and long COVID.

papers.title: Neuroendocrine signature of ME/CFS: Meta-analytic evidence for bioactive cortisol deficit and exaggerated feedback sensitivity
papers.authors: Woo TW, Choi YJ, Kim JY, Lee JS, Son CG
papers.summary: Cortisol is the body's main stress hormone. It is controlled by a chain of glands called the HPA axis (hypothalamus, pituitary, adrenal glands). This analysis pooled 46 studies with about 1,400 ME/CFS patients and 1,350 healthy people. Patients had lower cortisol in saliva, urine and hair. They reacted weakly to a hormone that should raise cortisol, and too strongly to a steroid that should lower it only a little.
papers.why: The stress-hormone system in ME/CFS seems blunted and over-braked. That could help explain poor sleep, brain fog and low tolerance for physical or emotional strain. Cortisol tests give researchers something concrete to measure.

papers.title: Facility-Measured Sleep Electroencephalographic Microstructures in Long COVID
papers.authors: Sun H, Dang R, Li P, Xiao W, Scott-Sutherland J, Sassower KC, Westover MB, Felsenstein D, Thomas RJ, Haack M, Mullington JM
papers.summary: Overnight brain-wave recordings (sleep EEG) compared 28 people with long COVID, 19 with ME/CFS and 28 healthy people. Both patient groups showed unusual details in their sleep brain waves. People with ME/CFS had some extra changes, for example slow "sleep spindles" that were out of sync, which the long-COVID group did not have.
papers.why: This gives an objective measure for the unrefreshing sleep that many patients describe. It also suggests that sleep is disturbed somewhat more in ME/CFS than in long COVID.

papers.title: The efficacy of exercise in patients with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: A systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Zhao L, Gou B, Zhang M
papers.summary: Pooling 17 controlled trials with almost 2,000 ME/CFS patients, exercise programmes improved fatigue, sleep and quality of life. They did not clearly improve heart and lung fitness or physical capacity.
papers.why: Exercise therapy is controversial in ME/CFS because overexertion can cause a crash. This analysis suggests exercise can ease some symptoms but does not fix the underlying limitation.

papers.title: Insights into Pathophysiological Pathways in ME/CFS Through Genetic Correlation and Mendelian Randomization
papers.authors: Wielscher M, Vincenzi L, Weninger WP, Schernhammer ES
papers.summary: Using genetic data from DecodeME (more than 15,000 people with ME/CFS), researchers looked for genes that ME/CFS shares with other conditions. They also tested whether some blood markers may cause ME/CFS. Having more mitochondrial DNA (the DNA of the cell's power plants) seemed to protect, while two markers of inflammation and blood clotting seemed to raise the risk.
papers.why: Because this is genetic evidence, it points to energy production, low-grade inflammation and clotting as likely causes of ME/CFS, not just consequences. That supports drugs aimed at mitochondria, inflammation or clotting.

papers.title: Identification of novel reproducible combinatorial genetic risk factors for myalgic encephalomyelitis in the DecodeME patient cohort and commonalities with long COVID
papers.authors: Sardell J, Das S, Pearson M, Kolobkov D, et al. (PrecisionLife)
papers.summary: Using an AI method that looks at combinations of gene variants, researchers re-analysed the DecodeME data. They found more than 22,000 repeatable combinations pointing to about 250 core genes involved in nerve signalling, inflammation, cell stress and calcium handling. 76 of these genes are also linked to long COVID.
papers.why: A follow-up analysis of DecodeME that turns genetic data into specific biological pathways. It names two existing drugs, ampligen and apremilast, as candidates for testing.

papers.title: Symptom clusters in ME/CFS reflect distinct neuroimmune and autonomic pathophysiological mechanisms: a translational model
papers.authors: Habermann-Horstmeier L, Horstmeier LM
papers.summary: The authors analysed symptom surveys from 748 people with ME/CFS in Germany. Symptoms that tend to occur together, for example brain fog, sensitivity to light and noise, and sleep problems, matched specific biological processes such as immune, nerve or gut problems.
papers.why: From the German APAV-ME/CFS study. It supports splitting ME/CFS into biological subgroups, which would allow more targeted drug trials.

papers.title: Imbalance of Excitatory and Inhibitory Neurotransmitter Systems in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Wirth KJ, Scheibenbogen C
papers.summary: This review looks at evidence that ME/CFS disturbs the brain's chemical messengers, the signals nerve cells use to talk to each other. That could explain brain fog and the feeling of being wired but tired.
papers.why: From the two leading German ME/CFS researchers. It connects what happens in the muscles with what happens in the brain, which supports the treatments they are developing.

papers.title: Pathophysiological mechanisms of post-exertional malaise: an integrative analysis based on the metabolism-immune-neuro interaction model
papers.authors: Jin H, An Y, Huang J, Luo T, Wu X
papers.summary: The authors propose how even light activity can trigger post-exertional malaise, the delayed worsening after effort. The cells' power plants falter, this sets off inflammation, and the inflammation reaches the brain and keeps the cycle going.
papers.why: A clear, testable explanation for the main symptom of ME/CFS that points to treatments aimed at energy metabolism and inflammation.

papers.title: Pipeline-optimized machine learning for chronic fatigue syndrome diagnosis: A lightweight, interpretable model using blood biochemical and metabolomic data
papers.authors: Li J, Cao H, Zhu Z, Zhai X, Xing A, Zeng S, Luo G, Sha Y, Li P, Li K
papers.summary: Researchers used blood results from a large UK database with more than 68,000 people, about 1,100 of them with chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS). A computer model predicted CFS very accurately from routine blood values such as urea, blood sugar and vitamin D. A genetic method suggested that six of these values may help cause the illness.
papers.why: Cheap routine blood tests could one day help flag CFS early. The model still has to be checked in other groups, and the CFS cases came from health records, not from strict ME/CFS criteria.

papers.title: Molecular hydrogen as a treatment for ME/CFS: a mini-review of clinical evidence and mechanistic rationale
papers.authors: Friedberg F, LeBaron TW
papers.summary: This short review looks at hydrogen-rich water, which is water with extra dissolved hydrogen gas, as a treatment for ME/CFS. It acts as an antioxidant, lowers inflammation and may help the mitochondria, the cells' power plants. Three small early studies found it practical and somewhat helpful for fatigue, with mild side effects.
papers.why: Cheap and low-risk, but the evidence is weak so far: the studies are small, not blinded, and rely on patients' own ratings.

papers.title: Pathophysiological, Translational, and Diagnostic Aspects of ME/CFS: A Focus on Skeletal Muscle Involvement
papers.authors: Fanò-Illic G, Coscia F, Gigliotti PV, Checcaglini F, Carraro U, Fulle S, Mancinelli R
papers.summary: A detailed review of what goes wrong in ME/CFS muscles: they get too little blood, build up harmful amounts of sodium and calcium, produce too much oxidative stress and lose their normal ability to contract. It also discusses how standard tests might detect these changes.
papers.why: It pulls molecular, cellular and clinical findings into one picture of muscle failure in ME/CFS and suggests diagnostic markers. That supports the muscle-focused approach of Wirth, Scheibenbogen and others.

papers.title: Charting the circulating proteome in ME/CFS using cross-system profiling to uncover mechanistic insights
papers.authors: Hoel A, Hoel F, Dyrstad SE, Chapola H, Rekeland IG, Risa K, Alme K, Sørland K, Brokstad KA, Marti HP, Mella O, Fluge Ø, Tronstad KJ
papers.summary: Researchers measured thousands of proteins in patients' blood and found many that differ from healthy people. They point to an overactive immune system and poor blood flow to the muscles.
papers.why: The largest blood-protein study in ME/CFS so far. It maps what goes wrong in the body and could lead to a blood test and new treatment targets.

papers.title: Immunoglobulin G complexes from post-infectious ME/CFS, including post-COVID ME/CFS disrupt cellular energetics and alter inflammatory marker secretion
papers.authors: Liu Z, Hollmann C, Kalanidhi S, Lamer S, Schlosser A, Basens EE, Nikolayshvili G, Sokolovska L, Riemekasten G, Rust R, Bellmann-Strobl J, Paul F, Naviaux RK, Nora-Krukle Z, Sotzny F, Scheibenbogen C, Prusty BK
papers.summary: Antibodies (IgG) taken from the blood of ME/CFS patients broke up the energy-producing structures inside blood-vessel cells and changed the cells' inflammatory signals.
papers.why: From Scheibenbogen and Prusty. Direct evidence that patients' antibodies harm the cells' energy supply, which supports antibody-removing treatments such as immunoadsorption and may explain why blood vessels work poorly.

papers.title: In Search of Lost Volume: The Potential Causes of Hypovolemia in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Wirth KJ
papers.summary: Klaus Wirth argues that people with ME/CFS often have too little fluid in their blood vessels (hypovolemia). He names three causes: faulty signals for keeping salt and water, leaky small vessels, and starved muscle cells that pull fluid out of the blood during activity.
papers.why: From Wirth (Mitodicure). It links low blood volume, dizziness on standing and the crash after activity in one explanation and supports his group's muscle and circulation approach. It is an early hypothesis paper that has not been peer-reviewed.

papers.title: Indistinguishable mitochondrial phenotypes after exposure of healthy myoblasts to myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome or control serum
papers.authors: Ryback AA, Hillier CB, Loureiro CM, Ponting CP, Dalton CF
papers.summary: A large study, planned in detail beforehand, tried to repeat a known 2016 result: that blood serum from ME/CFS patients changes how healthy muscle cells make energy. With blood from 67 patients and 53 healthy people and more than 1,700 lab measurements, it found no such effect.
papers.why: A careful failed replication from Chris Ponting's group, who also lead DecodeME. It casts doubt on a widely cited piece of evidence for a harmful factor in the blood and shows that the field checks its own results.

papers.title: Extracellular Vesicle Protein and MiRNA Signatures as Biomarkers for Post-Infectious ME/CFS Patients
papers.authors: Seifert M, Schäfers J, Douglas FF, Schwarzburg C, Boristowski D, Birke A, Klein O, Sotzny F, Rubarth K, Windzio L, Beez CM, Kedor Peters C, Wittke K, Scheibenbogen C, Greco A
papers.summary: Tiny particles released by blood cells (extracellular vesicles) carry their own protein and genetic signals in ME/CFS patients. Lower levels of one small RNA molecule (microRNA let-7b-5p) went with worse fatigue and pain.
papers.why: From Scheibenbogen's group. These particles could become a blood test for ME/CFS and help sort patients into subgroups for more targeted treatment.

papers.title: The potential causes of myasthenia and fasciculations in severely ill ME/CFS patients: the role of disturbed electrophysiology
papers.authors: Wirth KJ, Steinacker JM
papers.summary: Klaus Wirth suggests that muscle weakness, cramps and twitching in severely ill ME/CFS patients have one common cause. An energy-driven pump in the muscle cell membrane fails, which leads to too much calcium and unstable electrical signals.
papers.why: From Wirth (Mitodicure). His drug MDC002 is meant to fix exactly this mechanism, so the paper is the scientific basis for the planned MDC002 phase 1 trial.

papers.title: Large-scale investigation confirms TRPM3 ion channel dysfunction in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Sasso EM, Er TS, Eaton-Fitch N, Hool L, Muraki K, Marshall-Gradisnik S
papers.summary: Several laboratories confirmed that a tiny channel (TRPM3) that lets calcium into certain immune cells does not work properly in ME/CFS patients.
papers.why: Because independent labs found the same thing, this faulty channel is one of the most reliable biological signs of ME/CFS. It is also a possible drug target.

papers.title: Proteomic signatures in cerebrospinal fluid and their clinical associations in patients with ME/CFS
papers.authors: Bragée B, Li P, Meadows D, et al.
papers.summary: The study looked at proteins in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord. It found inflammation-related patterns that matched how ill patients were and whether they also had POTS, a racing heart when standing up.
papers.why: One of the first studies of this fluid in ME/CFS. These patterns could help sort patients into the right treatment groups.

papers.title: Temelimab versus placebo in patients with post-COVID condition
papers.authors: Nehme M, et al.
papers.summary: 203 people with lasting neurological post-COVID symptoms got temelimab or a placebo for 24 weeks. Temelimab is an antibody that blocks a protein made from old virus sequences in our own DNA. Fatigue improved about equally in both groups. The drug brought no extra benefit for fatigue, thinking, mood or quality of life.
papers.why: A large, careful trial (NCT05497089) with a negative result. It tested the idea that a reactivated retrovirus protein (HERV-W) drives post-COVID and ME/CFS-like illness and found no support for treating it. Other mechanisms, such as mitochondria, blood vessels or autoantibodies, remain in focus.

papers.title: Mapping the complexity of ME/CFS: Evidence for abnormal energy metabolism, altered immune profile, and vascular dysfunction
papers.authors: Heng B, Gunasegaran B, Krishnamurthy S, et al.
papers.summary: Comparing blood from ME/CFS patients and healthy people, researchers found several problems at once. Immune cells were short of ATP, the cell's fuel. Several types of immune cells looked less mature than normal. Blood proteins linked to clotting and blood-vessel reactions were raised, a sign that the vessel lining is not working well.
papers.why: One study that shows energy, immune and blood-vessel problems together in ME/CFS. These markers could help with diagnosis or serve as treatment targets.

papers.title: Exploring a genetic basis for the metabolic perturbations in ME/CFS using UK biobank
papers.authors: Huang K, et al.
papers.summary: Using UK Biobank data from almost 37,000 people, researchers linked specific gene variants to unusual blood chemistry in ME/CFS patients. Fat metabolism and messenger-substance (neurotransmitter) pathways seem to be partly genetically driven in the illness.
papers.why: A genome-wide look at ME/CFS metabolism in one of the largest health datasets. The genetic links could point to drug targets and explain why patients' cells behave differently.

papers.title: Development and validation of blood-based diagnostic biomarkers for Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS) using EpiSwitch® 3-dimensional genomic regulatory immuno-genetic profiling
papers.authors: Hunter E, Alshaker H, Bundock O, Weston C, Bautista S, Gebregzabhar A, Virdi A, Croxford J, Dring A, Powell R, Vugrinec D, Kingdon C, Wilson C, Dowrick S, Green J, Akoulitchev A, Pchejetski D
papers.summary: Researchers developed a blood test that reads how DNA is folded in three dimensions. In a separate test group it told ME/CFS patients from healthy people with 96% accuracy.
papers.why: One of the most accurate blood tests reported for ME/CFS, which has no objective test today. It also points to immune and brain-inflammation pathways as possible drug targets.

papers.title: Heightened innate immunity may trigger chronic inflammation, fatigue and post-exertional malaise in ME/CFS
papers.authors: Che X, Ranjan A, Guo C, Zhang K, Goldsmith R, Levine S, Moneghetti KJ, Zhai Y, Ge L, Mishra N, Hornig M, Bateman L, Klimas NG, Montoya JG, Peterson DL, Klein SL, Fiehn O, Komaroff AL, Lipkin WI
papers.summary: Immune cells from ME/CFS patients overreacted to signals from bacteria and viruses and made far more inflammatory molecules than cells from healthy people. This overreaction was linked to disturbed energy production and an imbalance of gut bacteria.
papers.why: A large study led by Ian Lipkin at Columbia University. It identifies the overactive first line of immune defence as a driver of symptoms and names existing drugs, including metformin and rapamycin, that could be tested.

papers.title: Initial findings from the DecodeME genome-wide association study of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Ponting CP, et al. (DecodeME Consortium)
papers.summary: The largest genetic study of ME/CFS, with more than 15,000 patients, found eight places in the DNA linked to the illness. Several of them are involved in fighting infections.
papers.why: The first strong genetic evidence that ME/CFS has a biological basis in the immune and nervous systems. It also gives new drug targets.

papers.title: Circulating cell-free RNA signatures for the characterization and diagnosis of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Gardella AE, Eweis-LaBolle D, Loy CJ, et al. (Hanson MR, De Vlaminck I)
papers.summary: A blood test that reads fragments of genetic material (RNA) floating in the plasma told ME/CFS patients from healthy people with about 77% accuracy. It also showed differences in immune cells and platelets.
papers.why: From Maureen Hanson's group at Cornell. A step towards an objective blood test, which ME/CFS does not have yet, and new clues about the immune system's role.

papers.title: Patient-reported treatment outcomes in ME/CFS and long COVID
papers.authors: Eckey M, Li P, Morrison B, Bergquist J, Davis RW, Xiao W
papers.summary: Almost 4,000 people with ME/CFS or long COVID rated how much more than 150 treatments had helped them. Both groups answered in very similar ways. Graded exercise therapy was rated least helpful.
papers.why: The largest survey of real-world treatment experience in ME/CFS and long COVID. It shows which symptom groups, such as autonomic or cognitive problems, respond to which drug classes, which helps plan trials.

papers.title: Plasma cell targeting with the anti-CD38 antibody daratumumab in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome — a clinical pilot study
papers.authors: Fluge Ø, Rekeland IG, Sørland K, Alme K, Risa K, Bruland O, Tronstad KJ, Mella O
papers.summary: In a small trial, 10 patients got daratumumab, a drug that removes the immune cells that make antibodies. 6 of the 10 improved, and several stayed better for one to two years.
papers.why: The first trial of this approach in ME/CFS. The clear and lasting improvement supports the idea that misdirected antibodies drive the illness. A larger trial is planned.

papers.title: Safety, tolerability and clinical effects of rovunaptabin (BC007) on fatigue and quality of life in patients with Post-COVID syndrome (reCOVer): a phase IIa randomised controlled trial
papers.authors: Hohberger B, Ganslmayer M, Harrer T, et al.
papers.summary: In a careful trial with a placebo group, a drug that neutralises self-attacking antibodies reduced fatigue and improved quality of life in people with long COVID.
papers.why: The first properly controlled trial to show a benefit from neutralising these antibodies. This supports antibody-targeted treatments that are also being studied in ME/CFS.

papers.title: Key Pathophysiological Role of Skeletal Muscle Disturbance in Post COVID and Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS): Accumulated Evidence
papers.authors: Scheibenbogen C, Wirth KJ
papers.journal: Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle
papers.summary: This paper collects the evidence that muscles in ME/CFS get too little blood and build up sodium and calcium, which damages the muscle cells' power plants.
papers.why: A core paper of the Wirth and Scheibenbogen theory and the direct basis for their drug MDC002, which aims at exactly this muscle problem.

papers.title: AI-driven multi-omics modeling of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Xiong R, Aiken E, Caldwell R, Vernon SD, Kozhaya L, Gunter C, Bateman L, Unutmaz D, Oh J
papers.summary: Researchers used artificial intelligence on four years of combined biological data (gut, blood, immune system, metabolism) to find ME/CFS biomarkers and predict how severe symptoms are.
papers.why: A data-driven map of the illness that could improve diagnosis and show new mechanisms.

papers.title: Deep phenotyping of post-infectious myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Walitt B, Singh K, et al. (NIH intramural study)
papers.summary: An in-depth study by the US National Institutes of Health found measurable differences in the brain, immune system and metabolism of people whose ME/CFS started after an infection.
papers.why: A high-profile government study confirming real biological changes. Its use of the term "effort preference" upset many patients.

papers.title: Multi-'omics of gut microbiome-host interactions in short- and long-term myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome patients
papers.authors: Xiong R, Gunter C, Fleming E, et al. (Hanson MR, Oh J, Unutmaz D)
papers.summary: A detailed gut analysis showed that ME/CFS patients lack bacteria that make butyrate, a fuel for the cells lining the gut. The pattern differed depending on how long people had been ill.
papers.why: One of the most careful gut-bacteria studies in ME/CFS. It supports the link between the gut and the illness and points to possible treatments.

papers.title: Endothelial dysfunction and altered endothelial biomarkers in patients with post-COVID-19 syndrome and chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS)
papers.authors: Haffke M, Freitag H, Rudolf G, et al. (Scheibenbogen C, Sotzny F)
papers.summary: The inner lining of the blood vessels (endothelium) does not work properly in many people with ME/CFS and long COVID.
papers.why: From Scheibenbogen's group. It supports the idea that poor blood-vessel function drives symptoms and points to treatments aimed at the vessels.

papers.title: Insights From Invasive Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing of Patients With Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Joseph P, Arevalo C, Oliveira RKF, et al. (Systrom DM)
papers.summary: Exercise tests with catheters in the blood vessels showed that in ME/CFS not enough blood returns to the heart during exertion (preload failure). The patients also had nerve abnormalities.
papers.why: From David Systrom's group at Harvard. A physical, measurable reason for exercise intolerance that points to treatments for circulation and nerves.

papers.title: Pathophysiology of skeletal muscle disturbances in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS)
papers.authors: Wirth KJ, Scheibenbogen C
papers.summary: The paper explains in detail how poor blood flow and a build-up of sodium and calcium could damage energy production in ME/CFS muscles.
papers.why: It describes the muscle mechanism behind the Wirth and Scheibenbogen theory and the reasoning for their drug MDC002.

papers.title: Insights from myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome may help unravel the pathogenesis of post-acute COVID-19 syndrome
papers.authors: Komaroff AL, Lipkin WI
papers.summary: A review arguing that long COVID and ME/CFS probably share the same underlying biology.
papers.why: It helped put ME/CFS at the centre of long-COVID research, which brought the field more attention and funding.

papers.title: Human Herpesvirus-6 Reactivation, Mitochondrial Fragmentation, and the Coordination of Antiviral and Metabolic Phenotypes in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Schreiner P, Harrer T, Scheibenbogen C, Lamer S, Schlosser A, Naviaux RK, Prusty BK
papers.summary: The paper suggests that when a common herpes virus (HHV-6) becomes active again, it can break up the cells' power plants (mitochondria) and push the body into a protective state with little energy.
papers.why: It links a viral trigger to the energy failure in ME/CFS and offers one way an old infection could cause lasting illness. Co-authored by Scheibenbogen, Naviaux and Prusty.

papers.title: Intravenous Cyclophosphamide in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome. An Open-Label Phase II Study
papers.authors: Rekeland IG, Fosså A, Lande A, et al. (Fluge Ø, Mella O)
papers.summary: In an open study without a placebo group, about half of the ME/CFS patients who got the immune-suppressing drug cyclophosphamide improved.
papers.why: An early sign that calming the immune system may help some patients. It needs a placebo-controlled trial, but fits the autoimmune line of treatment.

papers.title: A Unifying Hypothesis of the Pathophysiology of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS): Recognitions from the finding of autoantibodies against ß2-adrenergic receptors
papers.authors: Wirth KJ, Scheibenbogen C
papers.summary: The paper proposes one explanation that ties ME/CFS together. Self-attacking antibodies against receptors that control blood vessels lead to poor blood flow, so too little oxygen reaches muscles and brain.
papers.why: The central theory of Wirth and Scheibenbogen. It is the basis for their drug MDC002 and for the antibody-removal treatments now being tested.

papers.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the prevalence of chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis (CFS/ME)
papers.authors: Lim EJ, Ahn YC, Jang ES, et al.
papers.summary: This analysis pooled dozens of studies to estimate how common ME/CFS is worldwide: roughly 0.5 to 1% of people, depending on the definition used.
papers.why: Many millions of people are affected. That is a strong argument for research funding and care services.

papers.title: A nanoelectronics-blood-based diagnostic biomarker for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS)
papers.authors: Esfandyarpour R, Kashi A, Nemat-Gorgani M, Wilhelmy J, Davis RW
papers.summary: A tiny electronic blood test (the "nanoneedle") told ME/CFS patients from healthy people by how their cells cope with stress.
papers.why: From Ron Davis's group (Stanford, Open Medicine Foundation). A possible objective test for an illness that has none yet.

papers.title: B-Lymphocyte Depletion in Patients With Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial (RituxME)
papers.authors: Fluge Ø, Rekeland IG, Lien K, et al. (Mella O)
papers.summary: A large, careful trial of rituximab, a drug that removes B cells (one type of immune cell), found that it did not help ME/CFS patients overall.
papers.why: From Fluge and Mella's group in Bergen. This clear negative result ended hopes for rituximab and changed the direction of ME/CFS research.

papers.title: Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome — Evidence for an autoimmune disease
papers.authors: Sotzny F, Blanco J, Capelli E, Castro-Marrero J, Steiner S, Murovska M, Scheibenbogen C (EUROMENE)
papers.summary: This review collects the evidence that ME/CFS, at least in a subgroup of patients, behaves like an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the body.
papers.why: From Scheibenbogen's group and the European EUROMENE network. It shaped the autoimmune model behind much of today's treatment research.

papers.title: Cytokine signature associated with disease severity in chronic fatigue syndrome patients
papers.authors: Montoya JG, Holmes TH, Anderson JN, et al. (Davis MM)
papers.summary: Blood levels of several immune signalling molecules (cytokines) rose in step with how severe a patient's ME/CFS was.
papers.why: From a Stanford group. It links the immune system directly to how ill people are and points to inflammation-based markers and treatments.

papers.title: Metabolic profiling indicates impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase function in myalgic encephalopathy/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Fluge Ø, Mella O, Bruland O, et al.
papers.summary: Blood chemistry pointed to a blocked step in turning food into energy. A key enzyme, pyruvate dehydrogenase, seems to be held back.
papers.why: From Fluge and Mella's group in Bergen. A concrete, testable defect in energy production that could explain the exhaustion and could be a drug target.

papers.title: Metabolic features of chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Naviaux RK, Naviaux JC, Li K, et al.
papers.summary: The blood chemistry of ME/CFS patients showed a widely slowed-down metabolism, as if the body were in a low-energy survival mode.
papers.why: A much-cited study showing that ME/CFS is a measurable problem of how the body makes and uses energy, not a psychological one.

papers.title: Antibodies to β adrenergic and muscarinic cholinergic receptors in patients with Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Loebel M, Grabowski P, Heidecke H, et al. (Scheibenbogen C, senior author)
papers.summary: Many ME/CFS patients have raised levels of self-attacking antibodies against receptors that control blood vessels and the nervous system.
papers.why: From Scheibenbogen's group. A basic finding for the autoimmune theory of ME/CFS and the basis for treatments that remove or block these antibodies, such as immunoadsorption and BC007.

papers.title: Reduced diversity and altered composition of the gut microbiome in individuals with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Giloteaux L, Goodrich JK, Walters WA, Levine SM, Ley RE, Hanson MR
papers.summary: People with ME/CFS had less varied gut bacteria and signs of a leaky gut that lets microbes pass into the blood.
papers.why: From Maureen Hanson's group at Cornell. Early evidence linking gut bacteria to ME/CFS, which opened up ideas for diagnosis and treatment through the gut.

papers.title: Distinct plasma immune signatures in ME/CFS are present early in the course of illness
papers.authors: Hornig M, Montoya JG, Klimas NG, et al. (Lipkin WI)
papers.summary: Patients who had been ill for less than three years had a distinct immune pattern in the blood that was gone in people ill for longer. The illness seems to have stages.
papers.why: From Ian Lipkin's group at Columbia. Early solid evidence that ME/CFS is biological and changes over time, and a hint that early treatment might matter.

papers.title: Beyond Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: Redefining an Illness
papers.authors: Institute of Medicine (US) Committee (National Academies)
papers.summary: A major US expert panel concluded that ME/CFS is a serious physical disease. It proposed simpler diagnostic criteria and the name systemic exertion intolerance disease (SEID).
papers.why: An influential report that gave the illness medical recognition and changed how it is diagnosed.

papers.title: Neuroinflammation in Patients with Chronic Fatigue Syndrome/Myalgic Encephalomyelitis: An 11C-(R)-PK11195 PET Study
papers.authors: Nakatomi Y, Mizuno K, Ishii A, et al.
papers.summary: Brain scans showed signs of inflammation, meaning activated immune cells, in several brain regions of ME/CFS patients.
papers.why: Some of the first direct evidence of inflammation in the brain in ME/CFS, the "encephalomyelitis" part of the name.

papers.title: Inability of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome patients to reproduce VO2peak indicates functional impairment
papers.authors: Keller BA, Pryor JL, Giloteaux L
papers.summary: ME/CFS patients did two exercise tests 24 hours apart. On the second day they could not reach their first-day performance, an objective sign of the crash after exertion.
papers.why: An objective test for post-exertional malaise, important for diagnosis and for disability assessments.

papers.title: Myalgic encephalomyelitis: International Consensus Criteria
papers.authors: Carruthers BM, van de Sande MI, De Meirleir KL, et al.
papers.summary: An international expert panel set stricter criteria for diagnosing the illness, built around symptoms getting worse after exertion. It recommended dropping the name chronic fatigue syndrome.
papers.why: Widely used criteria in research and clinics that put the worsening after exertion at the centre of the diagnosis.

overview.intro: A short summary in plain language of what research shows about ME/CFS so far. It only uses the papers and trials listed on this site and is updated when new results come in.

model.title: How the pieces may fit together
model.caption: This is one leading model, proposed by Wirth and Scheibenbogen. Some steps are well supported, others are still being tested, and it may not fit every patient.

sections.title: What ME/CFS is
sections.takeaway: A serious, long-lasting physical illness. Its main feature is a crash after even small amounts of activity.
